title: Sunday Deep Dive: Eisenkot Gets the Mandate, a Leaked Russian Death Toll, and Iraq's Lights Go Out
bluf: The week's real shift was political, not military: US voters punished the Iran war, oil fell about 13% as traders priced in pressure for a deal, and on November 8 Trump told CNN new strikes are highly unlikely if Iran signs a strong agreement, even as minor US strikes continued. In Israel, Herzog handed Gadi Eisenkot the mandate three days early, but his road to a government runs through Avigdor Lieberman's veto on the Arab parties, which now hold a record 19 seats. Russia and Ukraine meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10 to 11 with heavier delegations on both sides, as hackers released what they say are Rosstat records showing up to 450,000 Russian war deaths. Below the headlines: a drone strike shut Kurdistan's Khor Mor gas field as winter starts, Paraguay's bank collapse froze about $380 million of pension money, and Taiwan detained a pro Beijing party founder three weeks before its local elections. Mississippi's Senate race is still uncalled, with Colom ahead by 2,574 votes per AP.

corrections.text: Edition 003 gave Scott Colom's Mississippi lead as 43 votes. That was an election night figure. AP had him ahead by 2,574 votes on November 7 with about 97% counted.
The elections calendar listed Haiti's first round for December 13. Haiti's electoral council postponed that vote in early October and set a first round for July 18, 2027. The calendar is fixed.
Edition 003 said Alaska's DOJ certification suit was dismissed; that stands, but DOJ has since appealed the dismissal (Alaska's News Source).

worldConditions.overall: Global risk is still set by the Iran war, but the trend this week bent toward talks: a Democratic House, falling oil and Trump's own words on November 8 all point at a deal track, while Russia's arms supply to Iran and continued minor strikes keep escalation live. Two negotiations open this week, Abu Dhabi on Ukraine and Eisenkot's coalition talks in Israel, and both could move the board. Iraq is the quiet risk: a militia standoff in Baghdad and a strike that blacked out Kurdistan's power just as winter arrives.

updates.update: No new confirmed tanker strike for November 7 to 8 surfaced in sources checked. The newest hard data (Lloyd's List, November 5) shows traffic slowed rather than collapsed, with outbound Gulf cargo the casualty, while Israeli press says a strike option remains open pending Washington. An FT report of Russian helicopter missile launchers for Iran adds a littoral capability relevant to the strait.

Delegations are now set: Umerov leads Kyiv's team with Budanov, Arakhamia and Kyslytsia, while Moscow added Deputy Foreign Minister Ryabkov and military officials under Medinsky. France says Europe will take part, the Kremlin says it will not, and Zakharova tied the Coalition 26.2 drill starting November 9 to that dispute. Hacker leaked Rosstat data claiming up to 450,000 Russian war deaths landed on November 8.

Mississippi is still uncalled: AP had Colom ahead by 2,574 votes on Saturday with about 97% counted, and Hyde-Smith has asked all 82 counties to set aside affidavit ballots. Alaska's ranked choice tally is November 18. Incoming Democratic chairs answered Stephen Miller's promotion with investigation pledges and a DHS records preservation demand.

Election security cases are accelerating three weeks before the November 28 local vote: prosecutors detained the founder of the Taiwan People's Communist Party over alleged CCP funding of ward chief races, a retired general in a separate Beijing money case got bail, and the MAC tallied 131 people targeted by transnational repression. Militarily, three more F-16V Block 70 jets arrived on November 8; no new large scale PLA drill was found in the window.

On November 6 the Gaceta reissued the Council of Ministers law to match Law 186, giving the central bank chief cabinet rank and requiring Council consultation before any resignation reaches the President. Law 186 enters force November 9; ministries then have 30 days to file implementation schedules. RSF's tally shows the press crackdown running on fines and warnings as well as detentions.

The hoax bomb campaign widened from airliners to broadcasters on November 6 (RTÉ, Sky, Nova TV), with emails signed 'Mikhail Andropov' claiming the airline threats too. ANSA reported the use of the Russian Men's State movement's name; its founder denies involvement. No official attribution yet, and no new information found on the supermarket fridge hacks.

Lula held an unscheduled macroeconomic meeting at the Alvorada on November 5 that included Mantega, Coutinho and heterodox economists alongside Alckmin and Durigan, while the Finance choice remains open. No new court filing by Flávio Bolsonaro was found in the window.

weekInReview.summary: Five editions in, the pattern of the week is that politics moved faster than the battlefields. The US midterms became a verdict on the Iran war, and both Washington and Tehran started talking like a deal is possible. Israel's coalition math, Ukraine's talks and Taiwan's elections all enter decisive windows in the next three weeks. The under the radar thread: wars are now hitting civilians through infrastructure (Kurdistan's gas, Sudan's grid, Iran's winter gas, Gulf fertilizer) rather than front lines.

shifts.soWhat: The deal track now has a clock: a lame duck strike or a framework before January. Antiwar voices left and right are watching for the first.

shifts.soWhat: Israel's coalition endgame (early to mid December) lands in the same window as Washington's Iran decision.

angles.title: Decapitation hardened Tehran instead of breaking it
angles.outlet: War on the Rocks (staff newsletter, with Cole Bucy podcast of Nov 5)
angles.argument: Killing Khamenei and other senior officials early in the war removed the leaders who knew the old rules and left survivors who believe they can outlast pressure, since forecasts of economic collapse have repeatedly failed. Iran also wants guarantees it will not be attacked during talks, which Washington may be unable to give. The result is a no war, no peace stalemate that Tehran rejects but Washington may tolerate.
angles.whyNonObvious: Leadership strikes are normally scored as wins; here they are the reason diplomacy is stuck.
angles.counter: The administration's stated approach, as described in the same piece, is to keep squeezing through the blockade and sanctions on the bet that a weakened regime eventually concedes.

angles.title: North Korea's troop surge was threat inflation; Pyongyang prefers laborers and shells
angles.argument: Kyiv warned of 30,000 to 100,000 more North Korean troops, but the force has stayed around 14,000 to 16,000. Pyongyang already has its combat experience and a $14.4 billion arms trade, and laborers earn hard currency with less risk of defections and casualty backlash at home.
angles.whyNonObvious: Western coverage repeated Ukrainian projections as likely; the quiet non event says more about North Korean cost calculations than about diplomacy.
angles.counter: Ukrainian officials, led by President Zelenskyy, maintain the risk is real, and the author concedes intelligence estimates differ and Russia could still ask for more troops.

angles.title: Airspace is the next front for isolating Taiwan
angles.argument: Pakistan's brief overflight ban on Taiwanese airlines went beyond anything Beijing does itself, and the March 2027 sunset keeps it available as a lever. Because Taiwan is shut out of the UN civil aviation body, it has little recourse if other China aligned states copy the move.
angles.whyNonObvious: Pressure on Taiwan is usually tracked through diplomatic recognition and military drills, not commercial overflight rights.
angles.counter: Pakistan's Defence Minister Khawaja Asif framed it as routine adherence to the One China policy, and the fast reversal suggests a bureaucratic overreach rather than a strategy.

angles.title: Don't blame the Democrats for the tech crash
angles.argument: The Nasdaq 100 had been falling for a month before its 6.5% drop on November 5, so pinning the rout on Democratic threats to AI data centers misreads a valuation correction already under way. Gold and silver rebounded from multi month lows even as rate hike bets rose.
angles.whyNonObvious: The dominant narrative ties the selloff to the election result; the timeline says the cracks came first.
angles.counter: Market coverage relayed by Cointelegraph, citing CNBC, tied the reversal directly to fears that Democratic policy would curb AI capital spending.

angles.title: The war is now a rate hike story
angles.outlet: BullionVault (market data); Bank of England decision
angles.argument: With Fed December hike odds near 77% and the Bank of England raising to 4.0%, the oil shock from the Iran war is producing a global tightening cycle at the same moment equities are falling. That squeezes indebted AI builders, households facing $4 gasoline and emerging market borrowers at once.
angles.whyNonObvious: Most coverage treats war, the AI selloff and monetary policy as separate stories; they are one feedback loop.
angles.counter: Bond markets show 10 year breakeven inflation at 2.24%, the softest since August, which traders read as a sign the Fed may not need to hike.

angles.title: Washington's trade wins in Vietnam may be shared with its rivals
angles.argument: Most favored nation clauses in Vietnam's EFTA and CPTPP agreements could extend any special access granted to US firms to European, Japanese, Australian and Canadian competitors. The telecom ownership cap is the clearest test.
angles.whyNonObvious: Bilateral deals are sold as America First wins, but legal plumbing in third party treaties can dilute them.
angles.counter: The author notes exceptions for earlier agreements and listed measures, and US officials have published no text, so the exposure may be small.

angles.title: COP31's electrification target could be a Trojan horse for gas
angles.outlet: Heinrich Böll Stiftung; Climate Home News (Nov 5)
angles.argument: Türkiye's pledge for 35% of final energy from electricity by 2035 does not require clean power, and civil society groups warn it could lock in gas and serve data centers before the 655 million people without electricity. The overshoot pathway the UN now accepts depends on carbon removal at a scale that does not exist.
angles.whyNonObvious: Electrification sounds green by default; the fight is over what generates the power.
angles.counter: The Türkiye presidency under Murat Kurum presents electrification as the practical path, and Climate Action Tracker data show even 35% would be a stretch over the projected 28%.

angles.title: Argentina is borrowing the Chagos playbook for the Falklands
angles.argument: By framing the Sea Lion oil field as a law of the sea violation, Argentina seeks a forum the UK cannot avoid, even though the tribunal cannot rule on sovereignty. The case may fail at the jurisdiction stage, but the tribunal has rarely narrowed its own reach.
angles.whyNonObvious: Coverage treats Malvinas as frozen rhetoric; the lawfare route is new and could affect investor appetite.
angles.counter: Rothwell himself argues the claim depends on unresolved sovereignty and could collapse at the first hurdle, unlike the Philippines' 2016 South China Sea case, which avoided sovereignty.

angles.title: A lame duck at home, not abroad
angles.argument: The midterms punished tariffs and the Iran war as pocketbook issues, but Trump keeps unilateral control of foreign policy until 2029. The bigger effect may be foreign governments hesitating for two years with a split Washington.
angles.whyNonObvious: It cuts against the common assumption that a Democratic Congress quickly constrains the war.
angles.counter: Alpert's own evidence points the other way in part: Democrats now control appropriations and can force a shutdown over policy demands; he also offers no Republican reading of the vote.

angles.title: Crude can fall and pump prices still won't
angles.outlet: AAA data via Travelers Today (Tom Kloza)
angles.argument: Only about 7 cents of a possible 18 to 24 cent decline reached the pump, and refined products may stay costly after crude eases. A peace deal would therefore lower gasoline prices more slowly than voters and politicians expect.
angles.whyNonObvious: Most coverage tracks Brent as the proxy for household pain; the bottleneck has shifted to refining.
angles.counter: AAA data show the national average still fell 7 cents in three days to a 2026 low, so pass through is happening, only slowly; the bigger risk named in the same report is a renewed US strike reversing the dip.

stateNarratives.outlet: Maria Zakharova Telegram channel (relayed by Prensa Latina, Cuban state agency)
stateNarratives.claim: The Coalition of the Willing drill Coalition 26.2, timed to start just before Abu Dhabi, proves Europeans have no place at the table; London and Paris want foreign troops in Ukraine as a platform to defeat Russia militarily, and any foreign contingent is unacceptable.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: France's foreign minister says Europe will take part in Abu Dhabi, and the coalition has described its planned force as post ceasefire reassurance rather than a combat deployment.

stateNarratives.claim: Europe has sent no security proposals and cannot even decide who speaks for it, showing indecision and unwillingness to engage; Russia will talk to Europe only at some later stage.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: European, US, Ukrainian and NATO officials met in Brussels on November 5, and Finland's and Norway's leaders phoned Putin directly days earlier.

stateNarratives.claim: The Russia and Ukraine meeting in Washington with Melania Trump was positive, and the 'Alyoshki' humanitarian operation was a joint success credited to her team and Russian ombudsperson Yana Lantratova; political and humanitarian tracks with the US complement each other.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Ukraine frames Oleshky as an evacuation of civilians from an occupied, shelled town Russia controls, and The Moscow Times ran an op ed warning readers not to accept Russia's account of it.

stateNarratives.outlet: Russian Defense Ministry (as headlined by The Moscow Times)
stateNarratives.claim: Russian forces struck power substations serving Ukraine's military and three vessels in the Black Sea.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Zelensky says Russian strikes have now damaged every Ukrainian power plant, and Kyiv says it holds Russian plans to destroy the grid before winter, which the UN reportedly flagged as a possible crime against humanity.

stateNarratives.outlet: Dmitry Peskov to Reuters (republished by Meduza)
stateNarratives.claim: Every resident of the 'new regions' had the chance to confirm their property rights; property left unregistered is lawfully ownerless.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Registration required Russian citizenship and Ukrainian documents were rejected as papers from a nonexistent country; Ukraine's Foreign Ministry calls the scheme a legal smokescreen for theft.

stateNarratives.claim: After the US midterms, Taiwan's DPP authorities are anxiously lobbying the new Democratic Congress, switch their values to suit whichever US party rules, have put the island's chip industry on the bargaining table, and cannot alter the course toward reunification.
stateNarratives.relatedTo: taiwan-strait; Taiwan's November 28 local elections; US midterm results
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Taipei's outreach to both US parties is routine and support for Taiwan in Congress has long been bipartisan. The editorial names no officials or events and offers no evidence for its claims about chip concessions.

stateNarratives.outlet: Global Times (opinion), quoting MFA spokesperson Guo Jiakun
stateNarratives.claim: One year after Prime Minister Takaichi said a Taiwan contingency could be a survival threatening situation for Japan, Tokyo has not corrected the remark, is rearming, and is weighing a National Security Strategy change that would let nuclear weapons into Japan in an emergency. Guo said Japan bears responsibility for strained ties and must correct its words and deeds on Taiwan.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Tokyo has said since November 2025 that its Taiwan policy is unchanged and has sent officials to Beijing to say so. The nuclear entry claim is presented without a Japanese source and should be checked against Japanese reporting on the security document review.

stateNarratives.outlet: China Daily Hong Kong, quoting MFA spokesperson Guo Jiakun and HK officials
stateNarratives.claim: Joshua Wong's 10 year sentence shows Hong Kong is governed by rule of law; Beijing backs the city's national security enforcement, and Chief Executive John Lee said Wong and Nathan Law undermined sovereignty and stability.
stateNarratives.relatedTo: Joshua Wong sentencing; Hong Kong National Security Law
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Rights advocates and US lawmakers say the conduct punished was peaceful lobbying of foreign governments in 2020, and Wong was weeks from release on an earlier sentence when this one was imposed.

stateNarratives.outlet: Iranian state television (IRIB), as reported by Iran International
stateNarratives.claim: Around November 4, the Embassy takeover anniversary, state TV broadcast live a staged mock hanging of an actor in a Trump mask and prison uniform beside a man in Revolutionary Guards uniform, as part of a campaign in Enghelab Square under a billboard reading 'We Will Kill Trump'. The framing presents the US midterm result as the punishment of Trump and his war.
stateNarratives.relatedTo: US midterms and the Iran war
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Iran International describes the campaign as a pro establishment staging; its own audience surveys the same week found Iranians saying they cannot afford emergency kits if war resumes, a sign the triumphal tone is aimed at a strained home audience. Trump said the war serves long term US interests despite the losses.

stateNarratives.outlet: Iranian officials, as summarized by Al Jazeera's live coverage
stateNarratives.claim: Tehran hailed the Republican midterm loss as a verdict on the war and urged Trump to end what it called the assault on Iran.
stateNarratives.relatedTo: US midterms; US and Iranian diplomacy
stateNarratives.counterpoint: Analysts quoted by Iran International argue the defeat could push Trump to escalate before the new Congress convenes in January rather than wind down, and Germany says Araghchi has been regularly seeking talks, which suggests Tehran's public confidence masks urgency.

stateNarratives.outlet: Gaceta Oficial and official statements at the law's approval (as summarized by Directorio Cubano; Granma and Cubadebate pages not reached)
stateNarratives.claim: Law 186 cuts administrative duplication by shrinking 27 central bodies to 21, and public bodies must now answer citizen complaints and petitions.
stateNarratives.counterpoint: The law sets no wages, fees or ration rules and does not say how many workers lose posts; CITMA scientists protested in August that their ministry was dissolved without consultation.

underRadar.headline: Iraq may move Iran's armed Kurdish opponents away from the Iranian border
underRadar.summary: Iraqi political forces are weighing a plan to relocate Iranian Kurdish opposition groups out of the Kurdistan Region to a center elsewhere in Iraq, discussed as an Iranian delegation met Nechirvan Barzani on November 8.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: It surfaces only as a background line in Iraqi and Kurdish outlets, and Western coverage of Iran's opposition focuses on Pahlavi and the diaspora rather than the armed groups on the border.
underRadar.coverage: Shafaq News only in sources checked

underRadar.headline: Occupied Zaporizhzhia: 7,000 properties declared ownerless, 521 of them hotels
underRadar.summary: Reuters counted more than 7,000 properties declared ownerless in occupied Zaporizhzhia, including 521 hotels and resorts, at least 77 already transferred. Title can be kept only with a Russian passport.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Property seizures move slowly and lack battlefield imagery, yet they will decide who resists any future territorial settlement.
underRadar.coverage: Reuters investigation, republished in translation by Meduza; little pickup elsewhere

underRadar.headline: Afghan opium output reportedly back near 1,500 tonnes
underRadar.summary: A UNODC estimate reported by Afghanistan International suggests 2026 production is about five times 2025, eroding the Taliban's main counter narcotics claim. The Taliban reject the figure.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Attention on Afghanistan is consumed by the Pakistan border war and the Iran conflict next door.
underRadar.coverage: Persian language and exile media; minimal Western pickup found

underRadar.headline: Taiwan used LNG purchases as a weapon against Papua New Guinea, and lost
underRadar.summary: Taipei halted spot LNG buying equal to a third of PNG's exports and still had to close its office, ending aid programs on the way out.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Pacific diplomacy rarely makes international news unless a formal recognition switches.

underRadar.headline: Credit bureau data helped decide who had to vote provisionally in Mississippi's Senate race
underRadar.summary: Mississippi used Experian consumer address data for voter roll maintenance; voters who never moved were flagged, marked inactive, and forced onto affidavit ballots now being judged county by county in a race within about 2,000 votes.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: National coverage frames the delay as slow counting, not as a product of a commercial data pipeline in list maintenance.
underRadar.coverage: Scripps local stations and NPR; Mississippi Today reported the credit data use earlier.

underRadar.headline: Chinese state defense firms now sanctioned under a Cuba order
underRadar.summary: CEIEC and a CETC International subsidiary were designated November 5 for supplying Cuba's military, alongside tanker owners in Cyprus and Panama.
underRadar.whyUndercovered: Coverage focused on the Cuban elite family designations rather than the China supplier angle.
underRadar.coverage: State Department fact sheet; law firm sanctions notes.
underRadar.source: State Department fact sheet (via Defcon Level)

conspiracies.claim: The midterms were stolen by fraud, possibly through hacked tabulators, as the opening move of a Democratic 'color revolution' (new hooks since Nov 7: a Michigan tabulator WiFi claim and a real Georgia memory card error)
conspiracies.whereSpreading: ZeroHedge (Kunstler column), X and Facebook posts by Patrick Colbeck, Wayne Allyn Root's livestream, Rumble prophecy channels such as Julie Green's
conspiracies.origin: Domestic right; Colbeck is linked to the Election Crime Bureau and backed by Mike Lindell
conspiracies.whyBelieved: A lopsided loss after polls were framed as a 'psyop' for months; long standing belief that the 2020 result was stolen; real, documented errors like Georgia's missed memory card show the system can miss votes.
conspiracies.caseFor: Counting errors do happen and are sometimes found only by audit, as Georgia showed this week; voter roll accuracy is a legitimate concern and the DOJ roll audit has not reported; Colbeck says a poll worker reported a WiFi signal.
conspiracies.caseAgainst: Michigan's Department of State said it received no report of a WiFi device and Colbeck declined to name the poll worker, agency or investigator; AP Fact Focus checked several Election Day rumors and found no supporting record; Georgia's confirmed error helped a Republican and was found by officials; the margins were large across many states.
conspiracies.unknowns: What the DOJ voter roll audit reports; whether Georgia's investigation finds similar missed cards elsewhere; whether any state certifies late.
conspiracies.watch: DOJ roll audit findings; Georgia secretary of state report; certification dates in close races such as Mississippi.
conspiracies.relatedTo: 2020 election claims; 'polls are a psyop'; SAVE America Act
conspiracies.audience: Core MAGA base, election integrity activists, Lindell network

items.headline: House Democrats move toward impeaching Hegseth as a fired admiral flips Nancy Mace's seat
items.summary: Yahoo News' running midterm coverage on November 8 reported the House could vote this week on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and that a Navy admiral Hegseth had fired won Nancy Mace's former South Carolina House seat. Details of the articles of impeachment were not collected this run.
items.assessment: An impeachment vote in the lame duck House would be symbolic (conviction needs 67 senators) but it puts the Iran war's conduct on the record before the new Congress takes over oversight in January.

items.headline: Mississippi's affidavit ballot pileup traces back to a state roll cleanup that used Experian credit data
items.summary: Scripps reported that thousands of Mississippians who showed up on November 3 found themselves marked inactive and had to cast affidavit (provisional) ballots, the main reason the Hyde-Smith and Colom race is still uncounted. The state had used Experian consumer address data to maintain its voter rolls; one voter said a clerk told him Experian placed him in another city although he has not moved in a decade. Experian says it has not served the state since 2025 and that its product supplied supplemental addresses and was never meant to validate voter records. The Secretary of State's office did not answer Scripps; NPR separately reported that Secretary Michael Watson's office could not say how many affidavit ballots remain, with over 9,000 processed by midday November 6.
items.assessment: Mississippi forces inactive voters onto provisional ballots while most states let them vote normally for years, so a commercial data error becomes a vote counting problem decided county by county. Whoever wins, the use of credit bureau data for list maintenance is likely to become a template fight in other Republican and Democratic states preparing for 2028.
items.source: Scripps News (via NewsChannel 5 Nashville); NPR via WHRO

items.headline: Hyde-Smith asks all 82 Mississippi counties to set aside affidavit ballots; Colom calls it unlawful
items.summary: Hyde-Smith's legal team wrote every county election commission asking that affidavit ballots be kept apart and each one's handling documented, citing state law on post election ballot handling. State GOP chairman Mike Hurst called it a standard preservation step in a close race. Colom's lawyers replied that state law has no provision for segregating counted affidavit ballots and that the demand threatens ballot secrecy. As of Saturday afternoon AP had Colom ahead by 2,574 votes, 49.1% to 48.8%, with about 97% counted; his lead has grown with each batch since election night. Hyde-Smith's campaign says thousands of votes remain in Republican counties.
items.assessment: Segregating affidavit ballots is the groundwork for challenging them one by one later, which matters because Mississippi has no recount procedure, so the fight moves straight to election contests in court. The conflicting margins are themselves a warning sign for narrative fights once county results reach the state next week.
items.source: WLOX; Mississippi Free Press; AP via MS NOW

items.headline: Alaska: a second 'Dan Sullivan' on the ballot drew about 3,600 votes in a race Peltola leads by 637
items.summary: With about a quarter of ballots still out, Mary Peltola led Senator Dan Sullivan 48.02% to 47.72% as of November 4 afternoon, a 637 vote gap, with ranked choice tabulation starting November 18. A Petersburg man also named Dan J. Sullivan drew roughly 3,600 votes. The Sullivan campaign, citing a New York Times report, says Democratic operatives helped put him on the ballot and calls it the biggest cheating scandal in state history; the Peltola campaign denies it. Per Just Security's tracker, DOJ appealed the November 1 dismissal of its Alaska certification suit to the Ninth Circuit the same day.
items.assessment: The namesake's votes are more than five times the current margin, so how his voters rank their second choice could decide the seat and gives the losing side a ready made grievance. Expect the ballot confusion claim, not machine fraud, to become the main Alaska narrative after November 18.

items.headline: Incoming Homeland Security chair orders DHS to preserve every record as Oversight Democrats tell Miller to 'lawyer up'
items.summary: Representative Bennie Thompson, expected to chair House Homeland Security in January, wrote DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin demanding preservation of all records, emails and contracts. After Trump named Stephen Miller chief of staff, Representative Robert Garcia, the likely Oversight chair, said Democrats will keep investigating Miller's conduct, with ICE use of force, including the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good earlier this year, named as a top priority. Hakeem Jeffries said Miller should be fired; Mullin's public answer was that deportations will continue.
items.assessment: Preservation letters are the first legal step toward subpoenas and make later deletion potentially obstruction, so they constrain the administration well before January. Putting the most investigated aide in the chief of staff office also gives the White House a stronger executive privilege argument against those very subpoenas.

items.headline: Free Beacon: Maine's new Democratic senator Troy Jackson backed bills for clients of a firm where his son lobbied
items.summary: The Washington Free Beacon reported that Troy Jackson's son Chace joined a lobbying firm founded by Jackson's former chief of staff in 2022, and that Jackson, then a Maine Senate leader, introduced bills benefiting that firm's corporate clients, including one that would have let a lender avoid the state's interest rate caps. The son stopped lobbying when Jackson left the state Senate. The piece names neither the firm nor the bills and carries no response from Jackson.
items.assessment: Right of center outlets are already building ethics files on the new Democratic class, which signals the counter oversight strategy Republicans will use once Democrats start subpoenaing the executive branch. Treat as an opening claim until the bills are identified.

items.headline: Hormuz traffic slowed but did not collapse under the October attack wave; old shadow fleet tankers are being pulled into legal Gulf trades
items.summary: Lloyd's List Intelligence, the shipping data arm of the London trade paper, counted 116 non Iranian cargo transits in the week of October 19 to 25, against 124 the week before, with the fall almost entirely in ships leaving the Gulf while inbound traffic stayed near normal. UKMTO, the British naval office that logs incidents, has recorded 144 events since the war began, and ships kept sailing in about three quarters of them. More than 50 tankers and gas carriers that were not under sanctions have shifted into Gulf trades, and tonnage that once served Iran, Russia and Venezuela is now being drawn into Gulf exports. The brief is moving to a fortnightly schedule, next due November 19.
items.assessment: The pattern of normal inbound and depressed outbound traffic means cargo is piling up inside the Gulf, which is exactly the leverage Iran's attacks are built to create without closing the strait outright. The quiet migration of former shadow fleet hulls into compliant trades blurs the line sanctions enforcers rely on, and it means the same ships could slide back to Iranian service if the war ends on Tehran's terms.

items.headline: Russia agreed to give Iran 90 helicopter mounted missile launchers, the Financial Times reports
items.summary: Iran International, the London based Persian language channel critical of Tehran, relayed a Financial Times report that Moscow agreed to supply 90 launchers for precision guided missiles that mount on helicopters. The same missiles are in wide use by Russian forces in Ukraine. Neither the launcher model, the helicopter platform, delivery dates nor payment terms were given in the relayed text, and no Iranian official response was reported.
items.assessment: Helicopter borne precision missiles are a littoral weapon, well suited to striking small and medium vessels in a narrow strait, so if the report holds this is a Hormuz capability rather than an air defense fix. It also shows Moscow choosing systems it can spare from its own war instead of the S 400 batteries Tehran reportedly asked for, a sign of how far Russia will and will not go.

items.headline: Belgium's defense minister says Tehran warned of 'dire consequences' if Reza Pahlavi spoke in Brussels
items.summary: Belgium's defense minister said on November 6 that Iran warned his government of serious consequences if it allowed Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of the last shah, to speak in Brussels. The event went ahead. The minister also said the war between the US and Iran affects Belgian economic and security interests. Iran International gave no detail on how the warning was delivered.
items.assessment: Belgium is the European state Tehran has pressured most successfully before, having traded a convicted Iranian diplomat for a detained Belgian aid worker in 2023, so a public disclosure by a sitting minister signals Brussels now judges the cost of quiet accommodation higher than the risk of exposure. Watch for a reprisal detention of a Belgian or EU national, which has been Tehran's usual answer.

items.headline: Tehran court sentences a social media activist to death over posts on X as executions pass 690 for the year
items.summary: A Tehran court sentenced Amirhossein Mousavi, a social media activist, to death over his posts on X, according to his lawyer. Separately, Iran Human Rights, an Oslo based monitor, counted at least 77 executions in October and 691 so far in 2026. These sit alongside the protester death sentences already reported from Mashhad and Isfahan.
items.assessment: A capital sentence for online speech alone, rather than for street protest or alleged violence, moves the red line from action to expression and is aimed at the diaspora facing influencers who shape the narrative abroad. The October figure is lower than peak months, which suggests the judiciary is pacing executions to avoid giving European capitals a reason to break off contact while talks are fragile.

items.headline: Saudi led coalition says Houthis tried to hit Riyadh; the Houthis now count 4,460 Saudi strikes since the latest escalation
items.summary: On November 8 the coalition spokesman, Turki al-Maliki, said two ballistic missile launchers were destroyed in Saada after an attempted Houthi attack on Riyadh, and that five missiles aimed at Saudi territory were intercepted since dawn. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed 91 Saudi air and missile strikes in 24 hours across six provinces and a cumulative 4,460 since the latest round began. Government forces claimed about 267 Houthi fighters killed, wounded or fled on fronts from Marib to Taiz. Nearly all figures come from the warring parties and are unverified.
items.assessment: A direct Saudi and Houthi air war, reignited since September, is running at a tempo that would lead the news in any other year but is buried under Hormuz. The open question is whether Riyadh's willingness to absorb missiles on its capital means it has concluded the Houthis cannot be bought off again, which would close the backchannel that kept Saudi Arabia out of the Iran war's line of fire.

items.headline: Israeli press: an Israeli strike on Iran is still possible, but no major US buildup has been detected
items.summary: Iran International relayed a Ynet report, from Israel's most read news site, that the Israeli military is waiting on Washington's next move and that a strike on Iran remains an option. The same report said no significant new American military buildup had been seen. It came as Trump weighed escalation against settlement after the midterm losses.
items.assessment: The timing matters more than the claim: Israel is now governed by a caretaker cabinet while a new prime minister designate negotiates, so any strike decision in the next four to six weeks would be taken by a government that may not survive, and by a leader with every incentive to show he still controls security policy.

items.headline: Herzog hands Gadi Eisenkot the mandate three days early; Netanyahu answers with a 'national unity' pitch that keeps Ben Gvir
items.summary: President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who leads the centrist Yashar party, with forming a government on Sunday November 8, ahead of the November 11 deadline, after 67 of 120 lawmakers recommended him against 46 for Netanyahu. Eisenkot has 28 days, extendable by 14, and said he will not swear in a government this week even if a deal comes sooner. His initial plan is a four party minority government backed from outside by the Arab list Ra'am and possibly United Torah Judaism. Netanyahu called for national unity rather than what he termed national suicide, while keeping Itamar Ben Gvir's Jewish Power in the package, which Yashar rejects.
items.assessment: Herzog had said days earlier that mutual vetoes made it unclear anyone could form a government, so moving early suggests he judged a quick handoff safer than a vacuum during a possible Iran escalation. The clock now runs to roughly December 6 or, with extension, December 20, which puts Israel's coalition endgame in the same window as Washington's own post midterm Iran decision.

items.headline: Arab lists hold an unprecedented 19 seats, and Lieberman's veto over them is now the main obstacle to ending the Netanyahu era
items.summary: Ra'am and the Joint List, the two Arab majority slates, won 19 seats in the October 27 election and both recommended Eisenkot. Avigdor Lieberman of Yisrael Beytenu, a member of Eisenkot's own bloc, refuses any government that leans on their support, citing their refusal to explicitly label Hamas a terror group, although both have condemned the October 7 attack. Lieberman says the only options are a 61 seat government including Haredi parties or a new election.
items.assessment: The Arab parties' record result is itself a product of the outgoing government's policies, and their leverage now exceeds what Ra'am held in 2021. If Lieberman holds his line, the practical effect is to hand the Haredi parties, who stayed neutral, the role of kingmaker, which means the price of ending Netanyahu's tenure may be paid in draft exemptions rather than in Arab inclusion.

items.headline: Lieberman, the loudest critic of Haredi draft exemptions, is reportedly negotiating with UTJ and Shas and may bend on conscription
items.summary: Shafaq News reports that Lieberman is in talks with United Torah Judaism and Shas, the two ultra Orthodox parties, and may compromise on military conscription of yeshiva students to build a 61 seat majority without the Arab lists. UTJ, with seven seats, declined for the first time in six elections to recommend Netanyahu but also refused to back Eisenkot. UTJ lawmaker Isaac Pindrus said the immediate priority is settling the status of Torah students.
items.assessment: If true, this is the most counterintuitive trade on the table: the politician who built his brand on drafting the ultra Orthodox could become the one who protects their exemption, in order to keep Arab parties out. UTJ's abstention is a message to Netanyahu that its votes are no longer automatic, and it raises the auction price on both sides.

items.headline: Drone strike halts all output at Kurdistan's Khor Mor gas field, cutting up to 2,800 megawatts of power
items.summary: Unidentified drones hit a sensitive section of the Khor Mor field in Sulaymaniyah province on November 8, and a source told Shafaq News that production and exports stopped completely. The Kurdistan Region's electricity ministry said generation would fall by 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts because several large plants run on the field's gas. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered a joint federal and Kurdish investigation, and the militia Asaib Ahl al-Haq condemned the attack. No group has claimed it.
items.assessment: The field is run by a UAE based consortium, and the strike landed the same day Kataib Hezbollah was publicly attacking Baghdad's oil contracts with Abu Dhabi's ADNOC and feuding with the prime minister, which makes it read as a message to Emirati capital whoever fired it. It also lands in the PUK's own territory days after the PUK walked out of the Kurdish government, deepening the Kurdistan Region's dependence on Baghdad for power heading into winter.

items.headline: Iraq's prime minister and Kataib Hezbollah square off over airport leases and his brother's wealth; Shia elders step in to prevent clashes
items.summary: Al-Zaidi cancelled three leases at Mosul International Airport held by companies tied to armed groups and reassigned them to international firms. Kataib Hezbollah, the most hardline Iran aligned militia, denied controlling the contracts and asked Iraq's Integrity Commission to investigate the finances of the premier's brother, Hassan al-Zaidi, while an allied MP filed questions on the premier's own wealth and advisers. Ammar al-Hakim and Humam Hamoudi, two senior Shia leaders, began mediating with the backing of the ruling Coordination Framework to avoid an armed confrontation. US envoy Tom Barrack, in Baghdad, said militia influence has no place in Iraqi institutions.
items.assessment: The fight is over money, not guns: airport concessions are part of the revenue base that lets factions survive any weapons deal, so the premier is attacking the business model rather than the arsenal. Barrack's public endorsement helps al-Zaidi with Washington but lets Kataib Hezbollah frame him as an American instrument, which is why Framework elders, not the state, are the ones brokering.

items.headline: Iraq's militia weapons deal is a numbers game: officials and factions cannot agree who signed what before a June 2027 deadline
items.summary: Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada had accepted weapons controls; Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada called that inaccurate and said it signed only a separate sovereignty pledge. Official tallies have moved from three of seven factions agreeing to five, with three said to have surrendered weapons, none named. The plan began October 1, the day after the US led coalition ended its mission, with handovers due by June 30, 2027, a date Washington has not accepted as binding. Kataib Hezbollah says the 'Islamic Resistance in Iraq' has halted operations inside Iraq until further notice but has signed nothing.
items.assessment: The Framework's own word for the process is 'regulating' weapons, not disarmament, which would leave arsenals in place under state paperwork, the same model Hezbollah long used in Lebanon. Kataib Hezbollah's pledge covers operations inside Iraq only, leaving room to act against US or Israeli targets elsewhere if the Iran war resumes.

items.headline: Nechirvan Barzani hosts an Iranian delegation as Baghdad weighs moving Iranian Kurdish opposition groups out of the Kurdistan Region
items.summary: Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani met an unnamed Iranian delegation in Erbil on November 8 to review a 2023 security pact under which Baghdad committed to stop Iranian Kurdish armed opposition groups from using Iraqi soil against Iran. Iraqi political forces are weighing a proposal to relocate those groups from the Kurdistan Region to a center elsewhere in Iraq, which the groups reject. Barzani said in October that the region warned them at the war's start they would not be allowed to attack Iran.
items.assessment: Tehran is using the war to finish a project it has pushed since 2022, when it struck these camps with missiles: removing the last armed Iranian opposition from its border. Relocation to federal territory would put the groups under the control of a Baghdad where Iran aligned factions hold sway, a quiet win for Tehran that gets no coverage outside Kurdish media.

items.headline: Turkey agrees to start handing its Bashiqa base in northern Iraq to Baghdad; Sinjar's Yazidi militia has placed its arms under state control
items.summary: After a meeting of the Iraqi and Turkish high level committee, al-Zaidi's office said Ankara will take steps toward a gradual handover of the Bashiqa Zilkan camp in Nineveh, Turkey's best known military base in Iraq. A Nineveh council security official told Shafaq that Turkish troops and vehicles have already partly left. The Sinjar Resistance Units, a Yazidi force long accused by Ankara of PKK ties, have put their weapons under state control, and a joint committee will verify the process in Sinjar.
items.assessment: Bashiqa has been a point of friction since 2015, so a handover is a real concession, and it is being paid for with Sinjar: Ankara gives up a base in exchange for Baghdad removing the armed presence Turkey calls a PKK corridor. That fits Ankara's wider settlement with the PKK, and it leaves Sinjar's Yazidis more dependent on a federal state that failed to protect them in 2014.

items.headline: Hackers claim Rosstat records show up to 450,000 Russian war deaths, released on the eve of Abu Dhabi
items.summary: Two hacker groups, the Belarusian Cyberpartisans (an anti Lukashenko collective) and Silent Crow (a pro Ukrainian group), say they took death records from Rosstat, Russia's state statistics service. The Cyberpartisans count at least 393,881 deaths explicitly tied to military operations from February 2022 to August 2026; Silent Crow puts it at up to 450,100 by adding non combat and unspecified deaths, rising from about 19,000 in 2022 to over 182,000 in 2025. Kyiv Post notes the records have not been independently verified and no methodology was published. For comparison, Mediazona's named count stood at 285,881 on November 6.
items.assessment: Leaking burns whatever access the hackers had inside a Russian state system, so the choice to publish two days before the Abu Dhabi round suggests they judged the timing worth more than the access. If the yearly curve is even roughly right, Russian losses are accelerating while territorial gains are slowing (Kyiv Independent math: about six deaths per square kilometer taken), which cuts against Moscow's claim that time is on its side at the table.

items.headline: Abu Dhabi line ups set: Russia adds Ryabkov and military officers, Kyiv sends Umerov, Budanov and Arakhamia, Paris says Europe will be there
items.summary: David Arakhamia, head of Zelensky's parliamentary faction, told the Kyiv Independent that foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov leads Ukraine's team, joined by himself, chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov and Serhii Kyslytsia. On November 7 Moscow said it would add senior diplomats and military officials, including Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov, to the delegation under Vladimir Medinsky. On November 8 French Foreign Minister Jean Noël Barrot said Europe will take part, contradicting Kremlin statements that Europeans are not invited; EU leaders are due to discuss representation on November 13. Budanov said these talks are neither the last nor final.
items.assessment: Ryabkov's portfolio is the United States and arms control, so his addition signals Moscow wants to fold Ukraine into a wider US and Russian strategic bargain, the format in which Kyiv and Europe have least weight. Ukraine answering with an intelligence chief and a former military intelligence head as chief of staff makes this a security services negotiation more than a diplomatic one, which fits the stated agenda of ceasefire mechanics and guarantees.

items.headline: Russia has declared 521 hotels in occupied Zaporizhzhia 'ownerless'; at least 77 have changed hands
items.summary: A Reuters review, republished by Meduza, found occupation authorities declared more than 7,000 private and commercial properties in occupied Zaporizhzhia region ownerless, including 521 hotels and resorts; at least 77 hotel properties have been transferred, 20 to state bodies. Owners could keep title only by taking Russian citizenship. Hotelier Denys Katyukha lost his 100 room Admiral hotel on the Sea of Azov to a state resort company within nine days and won a $5.1 million Ukrainian court judgment Russia ignores. Peskov told Reuters residents had a fair chance to register; Ukraine's Foreign Ministry calls it state organized theft.
items.assessment: Each transfer creates a new owner with a material stake in the occupation becoming permanent, which is a lobby against any return of territory that will exist before negotiators ever draw a line. The Hague based Register of Damage has about 195,000 claims and expects 6 to 8 million with no payout mechanism, so any deal that freezes current lines effectively launders these transfers.

items.headline: Mediazona names 350 Russian conscripts killed in Ukraine despite the Kremlin's pledge not to use them
items.summary: Mediazona, an independent Russian outlet that tracks losses with BBC Russian and volunteers through public records, published 350 names of conscripts killed in the war. It also has names of nearly 700 men who signed contracts during compulsory service, often under pressure or violence according to its reporting. Officially conscripts only guard border regions, and the Defense Ministry promised early in the war to withdraw them all.
items.assessment: Conscripts dying is one of the few Kremlin red lines that still moves Russian public mood, because it reaches families that never volunteered. The larger signal is the 700 contract conversions: they show the army is quietly turning the draft into a recruiting pipeline, which lets Moscow avoid a formal mobilization during talks.

items.headline: Moscow plans to let airlines keep flying unreturned Western leased jets through 2028
items.summary: Vedomosti reports a draft government resolution from the Transport Ministry that would extend until the end of 2028 the 2022 regime letting Russian airlines fly foreign leased planes and engines they never returned. Of 515 leased aircraft at the start of the war, 407 stayed in Russia and lessor claims were settled on 204 by 2025, leaving the rest in legal limbo. The ministry says the measure protects companies from 'unfriendly countries'.
items.assessment: Whatever the Kremlin says publicly about Abu Dhabi and US sanctions relief, its own bureaucracy is planning for Western aviation sanctions to last at least two more years. Draft regulations like this one are a more honest read of Moscow's planning horizon than Peskov's briefings.

items.headline: Kremlin says out loud that Armenia is de facto not taking part in the CSTO
items.summary: Asked about Armenia at his November 6 briefing, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Yerevan is in practice not participating in the work of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), the Moscow led military alliance of six former Soviet states. He said next steps depend on discussions inside the organization. Armenia froze its participation in 2024 but has not formally left.
items.assessment: For two years Moscow treated Armenia's freeze as a temporary sulk; naming it as a fact moves the Kremlin from denial to managing a loss, which usually precedes pressure through levers it still holds, such as gas pricing, migrant workers and the Russian base at Gyumri.

items.headline: Kraków mass shooting: nine dead including the gunman's family, prosecutors open a terrorism case
items.summary: On November 7 a 24 year old man identified as Michał O. drove through Kraków's historic center firing at random from his car with what appears to be an AR 15 style rifle, killing six people, among them a British man, and wounding 16 from Poland, the UK, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria. His parents and sister were found dead at home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński said initial findings point to very radical far right views, still being verified; the National Prosecutor's Office opened a terrorism investigation on November 8. Notes from Poland calls it the first mass public shooting of this type in a country with one of Europe's lowest gun ownership rates.
items.assessment: Tusk declared national mourning and President Nawrocki signed the decree, a rare joint act in the middle of the tribunal fight; watch whether that holds or whether the motive question (far right versus other) becomes another partisan front. With a Russian national among the wounded and a crowded information space, expect foreign channels to test competing attribution stories before investigators finish.

items.headline: S&P puts a price on Poland's institutional war: negative outlook, citing presidential vetoes and the tribunal standoff
items.summary: On November 6 S&P moved Poland's outlook to negative and cut its local currency ratings from A to A minus, calling it one of the most significant fiscal deteriorations globally. The deficit was 7.3 percent of GDP in 2025, the second highest in the EU, and S&P projects net debt above 70 percent of GDP by 2029. It named presidential vetoes and constitutional court tensions as constraints. Finance Minister Andrzej Domański pointed to the vetoes; President Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills, blames Tusk's government for budget chaos.
items.assessment: This is the first time a rating agency has explicitly tied Poland's borrowing costs to the cohabitation fight and the tribunal crisis, so both camps now have a number to hurl at each other before the 2027 election. The deeper strain is that Poland's defense buildup, Europe's largest relative to GDP, is being financed with debt, which is exactly the kind of slow cost a frontline state cannot easily sustain and Moscow can wait out.

items.headline: Poland's tribunal crisis splits the rule of law camp: 'not a coup', but the method is questioned
items.summary: On October 30 seven parliament elected judges entered the Constitutional Tribunal escorted by the state protection service, and judge Anna Korwin Piotrowska announced she was taking over leadership; President Nawrocki cut short a trip to Senegal. In a November 4 EUobserver op ed, law professor Alberto Alemanno argues the operation aimed to restore a lawful court rather than capture it, citing the EU Court of Justice's 2025 ruling that the tribunal is not independent and a May 2026 European Court of Human Rights order, but says it raises legitimate questions of method. The same day the International Commission of Jurists said the takeover contravenes international standards on judicial independence. A deputy prime minister has since floated a 'constitutional reset'.
items.assessment: The government's strongest asset was that European courts and jurists stood behind it; once a body like the ICJ criticizes the method, Brussels loses room to back Tusk loudly, and the 'coup' framing pushed by Le Pen and Farage gains a respectable citation. The S&P action two days later shows the dispute is now leaking into markets.

items.headline: Hoax bomb threats jump from airliners to TV newsrooms, signed 'Mikhail Andropov', with a Russian manosphere name attached
items.summary: On November 6 Ireland's RTÉ, Britain's Sky and Bulgaria's Nova TV received emails under the subject 'MESSAGE TO THE WEST' claiming a bomb would go off in 45 minutes; nothing was found, but RTÉ ran music and recorded messages for three hours and Nova evacuated its newsroom. The sender, signing with a name echoing Soviet leader Yuri Andropov, claimed responsibility for the previous week's airline threats (at least seven flights on November 3 and twelve on November 5). ANSA reported the threats were sent in the name of 'Fighters of Men's State', a reference to a Russian misogynist movement; its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov denies any role and says the group has not existed since 2021. European authorities have not attributed the campaign.
items.assessment: The signature is attribution bait: a Soviet spy chief's name and a defunct Russian far right brand point at Moscow so loudly that it could be a genuine taunt, a false flag, or freelancers borrowing a brand, and each reading demands different responses. The move from aviation to broadcasters looks like a cheap test of how different sectors' emergency protocols react, and RTÉ losing three hours of air shows the cost lands even when the bomb does not exist.

items.headline: Finland runs two tracks: its president calls Putin while its prime minister calls a total ban on Russians a logical next step
items.summary: Prime Minister Petteri Orpo announced the Foreign Ministry is preparing new entry restrictions on Russian citizens, including athletes, ahead of two NHL games in Helsinki next week, the Finlandia Trophy skating event on November 20 and 21, and a ski World Cup in Ruka on November 27 to 29. He described a complete ban on Russians entering Finland as a logical next step. The move follows an October Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling reinstating Russia's hockey team, which federations in Sweden, Finland, Latvia, Norway, Denmark and Czechia say they will refuse to play. It comes days after President Alexander Stubb and Norway's Jonas Gahr Støre phoned Putin.
items.assessment: Helsinki is pairing an open channel at head of state level with the hardest border posture in the EU, which makes the call harder for Moscow to read as softness and harder for critics like Denmark's Frederiksen to call appeasement. Sport is the test case because CAS rulings are opening doors that governments now have to close by visa law.

items.headline: Who speaks for Europe? Støre defends talking to Putin, Frederiksen is 'very skeptical', EU leaders decide November 13
items.summary: US, Ukrainian, NATO and European officials met in Brussels on November 5 on guarantees for Kyiv and a wider European security framework. Norway's Støre argued Putin should hear Europeans directly rather than through Trump's envoys, while Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she doubts Russia wants peace with Ukraine or Europe. Peskov said Europe has sent no proposals and cannot decide who represents it; France's Barrot said on November 8 that Europe will take part in Abu Dhabi, and EU leaders meet November 13 on representation.
items.assessment: Moscow's preferred outcome is to deal with Europeans one capital at a time, and the Nordic split hands it that. Whoever the EU names will shape whether a deal includes a European security treaty or just a US and Russian side arrangement that Europe has to live with.

items.summary: Two weeks after the October 25 election, Serbia still has no government; RTÉ reports the Student List took about 53 percent and 140 of 250 seats, with cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić and former basketball player Dejan Bodiroga floated for prime minister. In a November 7 column, former UK Europe minister Denis MacShane notes that movement founder Radomir Saičić called Kosovo temporarily occupied territory days before the vote, that its website calls Kosovo's government 'provisional institutions', and that its program names Russia a traditional partner on open questions including Kosovo. Srdanović says the movement is committed to EU integration and will respect agreements signed by earlier governments, without confirming the 2013 Brussels Agreement.
items.assessment: Western capitals cheered Vučić's fall as a democratic win, but on Kosovo the students may be less flexible than he was, because a leaderless movement that decides by assembly cannot easily trade away a national cause. That keeps Moscow's Security Council veto on Kosovo relevant to Belgrade even as the NIS refinery passes to Hungary's MOL.

items.headline: Taiwan detains the founder of the tiny Taiwan People's Communist Party over alleged Beijing money in neighborhood chief races
items.summary: Prosecutors in Tainan and Hsinchu searched premises on November 7 and announced on November 8 that Lin Te-wang, who founded the Taiwan People's Communist Party in 2017, is in detention without outside contact. They allege he took funding and instructions from the Chinese Communist Party to run for ward (li) chief in Tainan's Xinying District and to bankroll a party colleague, Chen Zhen-zhou, in a Hsinchu ward race. Investigators say the pair recruited voters for all expenses paid trips to China, possibly as vote buying; 13 suspects were questioned in Tainan. Chen was freed on NT$50,000 bail and prosecutors plan to appeal.
items.assessment: The alleged target is the smallest elected office in Taiwan, the ward chief, which suggests influence work aimed at the grassroots networks that deliver turnout rather than at headline races. Expect Beijing and parts of the opposition to cast the steady run of Anti-Infiltration Act cases before November 28 as DPP lawfare, so the conviction rate after the vote matters more than the arrests now.

items.headline: Taiwan counts 131 people targeted by Chinese transnational repression and moves to write the offense into law
items.summary: Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Minister Liang Wen-chieh told a legislative committee on November 5 that 131 Taiwanese were targeted in 149 incidents between 2005 and 2026, through nine methods ranging from physical attacks and criminal prosecution to border bans, sanctions and digital harassment. He cited assaults on Japanese commentator Akio Yaita and Taiwanese comedian Huang Yi-hao as suspected CCP linked cases. Justice Minister Cheng Ming-chien said current law falls short: nothing bans reporting Taiwanese to China's online informant portal, and the stalking law does not cover politically motivated following. The justice ministry is drafting Anti-Infiltration Act amendments to define transnational repression and add asset confiscation.
items.assessment: Turning a diplomatic grievance into a statutory crime gives Taipei a legal template that Japan, whose citizen Yaita was among the cited victims, and other democracies could copy. It also creates a new category of prosecutions that Beijing will cite as proof of DPP hostility during the campaign.

items.headline: Taiwan shuts its Papua New Guinea office and cuts off LNG spot buying; Washington voices concern
items.summary: Taiwan's foreign ministry said on November 6 it will close its representative office in Papua New Guinea and withdraw all staff after Port Moresby renewed a demand, first made in July, that the office go. Taipei is also ending technical and medical missions and scholarships and has stopped spot purchases of PNG liquefied natural gas; it says its buying equals about a third of PNG's exports and that it had planned roughly 500,000 tonnes in the first half of 2026. The ministry blamed Chinese political and economic pressure, though the report offers no evidence on PNG's own reasoning. The US expressed concern about the forced closure on November 8.
items.assessment: This is a rare case of Taiwan using commercial leverage punitively, and it failed to save the office, which shows how little energy purchases weigh against Beijing's offer in the Pacific. Watch whether Washington turns its concern into pressure on Port Moresby, where it holds a defense cooperation agreement.

items.headline: Beijing writes its reading of UN Resolution 2758 into a joint statement with Gabon; Taipei protests
items.summary: After talks between Xi Jinping and Gabonese President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, China's foreign ministry released a joint statement on November 6 in which Gabon reaffirmed the One China principle. Taiwan's foreign ministry said on November 7 that the text distorted UN General Assembly Resolution 2758 of 1971, which addresses China's UN seat and does not mention Taiwan. Taipei accused Beijing of routinely using bilateral meetings to get partners to sign language that undermines the Republic of China's sovereignty.
items.assessment: Each such statement adds to a growing stack of state practice that Beijing can later present at the UN as near universal acceptance of its 2758 interpretation, which is why Taipei now answers even small partners like Gabon. The legal fight over 2758 matters more for Taiwan's access to UN agencies than formal recognitions do.

items.headline: Joshua Wong gets 10 more years for foreign collusion, weeks before he was due out
items.summary: Hong Kong High Court judge Tam Yiu-ho sentenced activist Joshua Wong on November 5 to 10 years for conspiring with foreign forces under the 2020 National Security Law, starting from 13 years and discounting for his September guilty plea. The case covers July to November 2020, when prosecutors say he worked with exiled activist Nathan Law to seek foreign sanctions. Wong had been due for release in January from his subversion sentence; he will now be about 40 on release around 2036. Police national security chief Steve Li urged Nathan Law to return and surrender; US Rep. John Moolenaar and Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council called for his release.
items.assessment: The timing means a second prosecution for 2020 conduct kept the best known face of the 2019 movement from walking free, a signal to exiles that old advocacy remains chargeable. Taiwan's MAC reaction folds the case into its own campaign messaging on what unification would mean, three weeks before local elections.

items.headline: Beijing's spy agency turns Japan's corporate data breach wave into a public lesson
items.summary: China's Ministry of State Security said on November 8 that more than 115 million records were reportedly compromised in Japan in six weeks from September to mid October, including over 22 million customer records from one unnamed software company and millions of restaurant membership records. It argued that such everyday data lets foreign intelligence services profile and target people, and blamed over collection, slow patching, weak access controls and outsourced suppliers. It named no companies and the figures are unverified.
items.assessment: The MSS is using a rival's misfortune for domestic compliance messaging and, implicitly, to frame Japan as a soft target, at a moment when Beijing is running a year long pressure campaign on Tokyo over Taiwan. Analysts tracking Japanese breaches can treat the 115 million figure as a claim to check against Japanese regulator data.

items.headline: New Zealand election: Labour wins the most votes, National wins the most seats, and the government survives by one seat on preliminary counts
items.summary: Electoral Commission preliminary results for the November 7 vote give Labour 29.36 percent (710,330 votes) and National 29.21 percent (706,680), but National takes 42 seats to Labour's 36 because it won 42 electorates, producing an enlarged 131 seat parliament where 66 is a majority. The governing National, ACT and NZ First bloc has 67 seats; Labour, Greens and Te Pāti Māori have 57, or 64 with the new Opportunity Party's 7. About 399,365 special votes (roughly 14 percent of the total) are uncounted and official results are due November 27, with the government in caretaker mode until then. Turnout was an estimated 74.6 percent, down from 78.2 percent in 2023.
items.assessment: A one seat margin with 399,000 specials outstanding is fragile: in 2023 special votes cost National two seats, so Opportunity, not NZ First, may end up holding the balance. The vote and seat split, which Wikipedia's tally notes has not happened since 1981, hands the losing side a legitimacy argument and will likely revive calls to abolish the overhang rule.

items.headline: New Zealand's overhang turns a vote splitting campaign and a new party into the story; senior National ministers fall out
items.summary: RNZ's election coverage on November 8 debated whether the overhang was artificially created by Harry Mowbray's Split Your Vote campaign, which urged voters to give electorate votes and party votes to different parties, while another analysis argued the campaign did not explain National winning two of three general electorates. Because National won more electorates than its party vote entitles it to, list MPs including deputy leader and Finance Minister Nicola Willis and Speaker Gerry Brownlee miss out on preliminary numbers, and Chris Bishop lost Hutt South to Labour. Luxon said he would build a relationship with Opportunity and call its leader Qiulae Wong; before the vote Wong said Opportunity would talk first to the party with most seats and would not back a government with Winston Peters as foreign minister.
items.assessment: Opportunity's stated condition collides directly with the current coalition, where Peters holds foreign affairs, so any deal that needs Opportunity could reshape New Zealand's China and Pacific diplomacy. A finance minister losing her seat to her own party's electorate success is the kind of mechanical absurdity that tends to drive electoral law change.

items.headline: North Korea's munitions chief speaks for the nuclear program, then the military fires several missile types at once
items.summary: On November 2 Kim Jeong-sik, first vice director of the Workers' Party Munitions Industry Department, condemned Iron Mace, a closed South Korea and US tabletop drill on integrating US nuclear forces with Seoul's conventional forces, as proof Washington plans a nuclear attack. Seoul's Unification Ministry called it unusual for a munitions official to issue such a statement. On November 4 the North fired several missiles from the Sondok area, and KCNA said it tested a new air defense missile and ran a fire strike drill. Stars and Stripes notes the FBI blames Pyongyang for stealing over $6 billion in crypto from Binance, which the North denies, and that the US, EU and Australia added sanctions last week.
items.assessment: Analysts quoted by Kyunghyang read the munitions chief's voice two ways: a push to field tactical nuclear weapons, or an opening bid to put suspension of joint drills on the table if Trump and Kim meet. A $6 billion theft, if confirmed, would make cyber crime a bigger revenue line than most of the North's legal trade and blunts the sanctions now being added.

items.headline: Malaysia: UMNO pays Najib's RM50 million fine and he goes home under house arrest, splitting the unity government
items.summary: UMNO's secretary general confirmed the party paid former prime minister Najib Razak's RM50 million fine, and the High Court ordered house arrest once it was settled; Najib left Kajang Prison and his residence was declared a prison. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said he disagreed with UMNO paying but called it the party's decision, while the Attorney General's Chambers sought to put the house arrest on hold and DAP leader Anthony Loke said his resignation would take effect when Najib got home. Sarawak's state election is set for December 12.
items.assessment: A coalition partner paying a convicted leader's fine tests whether Anwar's reform brand survives his dependence on UMNO, and a Loke resignation would expose the DAP's Chinese Malaysian base to the cost of that bargain before Sarawak votes. These are headline level reports only and need confirmation of what exactly Loke is resigning from.

items.headline: The Hormuz war shows up in Southeast Asian prices: Thai inflation breaches target, Philippine inflation at a three year high
items.summary: Thai inflation rose to 3.9 percent, breaching the Bank of Thailand's target for the first time in over three years, and Philippine inflation hit a three year high, according to regional headlines on November 6. Indonesia meanwhile reported faster third quarter growth and forecast 5.4 percent for 2026, and analysts expect Bank Negara Malaysia to raise rates by 25 basis points in 2027.
items.assessment: Import dependent ASEAN economies are absorbing the oil shock from the Gulf war through food and fuel prices, which puts central banks that were cutting into a bind and raises protest risk in places like the Philippines. Thailand's Anutin government, courting US data center money, now has less room for subsidies.

items.headline: Myanmar's junta sets April 4, 2027 by elections to extend its parliament into contested areas; Tokyo keeps it on a blacklist
items.summary: Myanmar authorities announced by elections for April 4, 2027, framed as expanding parliament's reach, and said they were confident of holding territory. Tokyo rejected a Myanmar request to be removed from a blacklist, Laos and Myanmar agreed to tighten border security, and Bangladesh reported rescuing Rohingya refugees during a gun battle on the border.
items.assessment: By elections let the military claim it is closing the gaps left by its earlier vote where fighting prevented polling, and each new seat becomes an argument for ASEAN normalization. Japan, usually the softest major donor on Naypyidaw, holding the line is a meaningful signal.

items.headline: Philippines: Beijing accuses Philippine politicians of intolerable conduct as Manila counts on the new Democratic Congress for military aid
items.summary: China accused Philippine politicians of conduct it called intolerable as tensions rose, while a Philippine envoy said the incoming Democratic led US Congress will sustain military aid, according to November 6 regional headlines. Rappler's maritime disputes page carries reports on Taiwan calling a Chinese trawler seizure psychological warfare and experts seeking to price environmental damage in the West Philippine Sea, but its items are undated.
items.assessment: Manila is moving fast to reassure itself that aid survives the change in Washington, which suggests real anxiety that a Democratic House will tie security money to human rights or budget fights. Beijing targeting named politicians rather than the government points to pressure on individual lawmakers ahead of the 2028 cycle.
