items.headline: UNODC puts Afghan opium at nearly 1,500 tonnes in 2026, about five times last year, as Doha Process drug talks open in Termez
items.summary: Afghanistan International reported that the UN Office on Drugs and Crime estimated 2026 Afghan opium production at nearly 1,500 tonnes, up from about 300 tonnes in 2025; the Taliban interior ministry rejected the report. A counter narcotics working group of the Doha Process, the UN led track for engaging the Taliban, opened a two day meeting in Termez, Uzbekistan, on November 5. The same outlet reported the EU saying it has not recognized the Taliban and has put five individuals on its human rights sanctions list.
items.assessment: If the UN figure holds, the 2022 poppy ban that was the Taliban's main selling point to donors is unraveling, possibly because a cash strapped regime at war with Pakistan cannot afford to enforce it. Holding the talks in Termez, on the main bridge into Central Asia, reflects where the trafficking pressure lands.

items.headline: Pakistan arrests an Afghan Taliban member in Kurram as Rubio publicly backs Islamabad's terrorism complaint
items.summary: Pakistani media said security forces arrested Qari Waqas, also called Qudoos, described as an Afghan Taliban member, while he tried to enter Kurram district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. At the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged Pakistan's concerns about terrorism from Afghanistan. Long War Journal, citing a New York Times report of October 24, says Pakistani military and intelligence officials have reached out to Afghan anti Taliban resistance groups, which Pakistan denies.
items.assessment: Washington voicing Islamabad's case while Pakistan reportedly courts the armed Afghan opposition points to a slow drift toward a proxy contest on the border, with the US quietly siding with Pakistan. The Taliban's own response has been to suspend trade, which pushes Afghan commerce north toward Central Asia and Iran.
items.source: Afghanistan International; FDD's Long War Journal

items.headline: Former senior statisticians question why India's 2027 Census asks for Aadhaar, voter ID and passport numbers
items.summary: Writing in The Wire on November 7, three retired officials, including a former director general of the statistics ministry and a former agriculture secretary, note that the August 14 gazette notification lists 40 questions, including Aadhaar, voter ID, passport and mobile numbers. They argue these identifiers serve no statistical purpose, conflict with the confidentiality in Section 15 of the Census Act, and could cause undercounts among migrants. The Hindu reported that a UP enumerator training discussed persuading people to share Aadhaar as citizenship proof, which census officials denied.
items.assessment: Linking census records to identity documents would let the state cross check the population count against voter rolls, which is why critics see it as connected to the contested voter roll revisions. The fact that the warning comes from retired statistics insiders, not opposition politicians, gives it more weight.

items.headline: Arunachal party says Delhi cites China to push the Siang mega dam while staying quiet on Chinese incursions
items.summary: Kaling Jerang, vice president of the People's Party of Arunachal, a former BJP ally, told The Wire on November 6 that the government invokes Chinese dam building to justify the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project, which his Adi community largely opposes, while denying PLA encroachment near Taksing in Upper Subansiri. His party's fact finding team reported year round PLA activity versus seasonal Indian patrols and locals losing yak grazing grounds. Chief Minister Pema Khandu acknowledged on October 29 that transgressions occur along an undefined border, and the ITBP chief said on October 22 that standoffs exist at more than one point.
items.assessment: Official admissions of multiple active standoffs contrast with the public line of a stable border after the India and China thaw, and Delhi using the China threat selectively to override local opposition to a dam could feed tribal unrest in a sensitive frontier state.

items.headline: Central Asian capitals bid to host UN security offices; Tokayev's idea of Russian observer status in the Turkic bloc draws Turkish pushback
items.summary: Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev offered at an Aqaba Process summit in Astana to host a regional UN counterterrorism office, and Kazakhstan's interior ministry proposed a UNODC cybercrime center in Astana. A Turkish ruling party official questioned President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's proposal to give Russia observer status in the Organization of Turkic States, citing language criteria.
items.assessment: Hosting UN bodies is a cheap way for Tashkent and Astana to buy international buy in for their sovereignty and draw donor money, and they are now competing for it. Tokayev offering Moscow a seat in the Turkic club, and Ankara balking, shows Kazakhstan still hedges toward Russia while Turkey wants the bloc as its own space.

items.headline: Kazakhstan asks Russia to reopen the Druzhba oil route to Germany after a six month halt; Uzbekistan plans to double uranium output
items.summary: Astana formally asked Moscow to restore oil shipments to Germany through the Druzhba pipeline after six months of suspension, according to The Times of Central Asia. Uzbekistan separately plans to raise uranium production to 15,000 tonnes a year by 2030, and its cotton harvest passed 5 million tonnes for the first time since independence.
items.assessment: Kazakh crude to Germany via Russian pipes is one of the few remaining East to West energy links, and Moscow's control of the tap is leverage over both Astana and Berlin. Uzbek uranium growth matters for Western utilities trying to cut reliance on Russian enrichment and fuel.

items.headline: Before Law 186 takes effect, Havana rewrites the Council of Ministers rules: central bank chief joins the cabinet and resignations get a new filter
items.summary: On November 6 the Gaceta Oficial (Cuba's official legal journal) published a harmonized text of Law 134, the 2020 law that governs the Council of Ministers, folding in the changes made by Law 186. The head of the Banco Central de Cuba is now a full Council member with ministerial rank, and a deputy prime minister may now hold only a ministry or the central bank, no longer an institute. The Prime Minister must also consult the full Council before passing any resignation up to the President, who then decides alone.
items.assessment: The resignation clause matters more than the headline mergers: during a one year reshuffle in which ministers lose portfolios, exits now pass through a collective filter first, which makes quiet departures and defections from the top harder. Putting the central bank chief at the cabinet table also signals that monetary and currency decisions will be handled as political ones, not technical ones.
items.source: CubaHeadlines (English edition of CiberCuba), citing Gaceta Oficial Special Edition No. 23 of 2026

items.headline: Law 186 abolishes the Domestic Trade ministry and moves the ration book's registry into a trade and foreign investment ministry
items.summary: The full text of Law 186 drops the Ministerio del Comercio Interior (MINCIN) as an independent body. Its job, including the consumer registry that underpins the libreta (the monthly ration book), goes to the new Ministerio de Comercio e Inversión Extranjera, which also issues commercial licenses and runs foreign investment policy. The law does not abolish the ration book or change quotas, and consumer protection is parked in the same ministry until another body is named. Ministries have 30 days from November 9 to file implementation schedules and one year to finish.
items.assessment: Nothing changes for households on paper, but the ration system now sits inside a ministry whose mission is attracting capital, so any future cut or phase out can come by ministerial resolution instead of a new law debated in the National Assembly. Economist Pedro Monreal had already warned in June against dissolving MINCIN; watch the 30 day implementation schedules for the first concrete signal.

items.headline: Beyond Yoani Sánchez: a CubaNet reporter is fined under Decree Law 370 and another's phone comes back disabled
items.summary: Reporters Without Borders (RSF) logged three journalist detentions in four days in Havana. CubaNet and ABC correspondent Camila Acosta was handcuffed on November 3 and released with an official warning over a video identifying a man she says is a security agent; her phone was returned unusable. CubaNet contributor Adelth Bonne Gamboa, held on November 2, says he was beaten, lost his equipment and was fined 3,000 pesos by the Ministry of Communications under Decree Law 370, the rule that penalizes online publications. Henry Constantín, director of La Hora de Cuba, has been jailed in Camagüey since September 16 and spent 15 days in a punishment cell, according to his partner.
items.assessment: The pattern is administrative rather than criminal: short detentions, warnings, fines and disabled phones raise the cost of reporting without creating trials that draw foreign pressure. That fits a government that just met US officials and wants to avoid new names for sanctions lists.

items.headline: Off the agenda: Lula convenes Mantega, Coutinho and heterodox economists at the Alvorada as markets wait for a Finance pick
items.summary: On November 5 the reelected president held a meeting on the macroeconomic outlook at the Palácio da Alvorada that was not on his public schedule. Present were Vice President Geraldo Alckmin, Finance Minister Dario Durigan, Casa Civil chief Miriam Belchior, Planning Minister Bruno Moretti, Management Minister Esther Dweck, former finance ministers Fernando Haddad and Guido Mantega, BNDES head Aloizio Mercadante, former BNDES head Luciano Coutinho, economist Laura Carvalho and businessman Eduardo Moreira. Lula also had a meeting of the critical minerals council the same day.
items.assessment: Markets fell hard after the October 25 runoff, and the market friendly answer floated in the press was Alckmin at Finance. Seating Mantega, Coutinho, Carvalho and Moreira at the table suggests Lula is weighing a growth first fourth term, which would deepen the selloff if it shows in the Finance choice; the absence of any fiscal hawk on the list is the signal.

items.headline: Cabinet rule for the fourth term: ministries go to parties that vote with the government, not to the biggest benches
items.summary: Lula plans to tie each party's share of ministries to its record of backing government bills in Congress, with appointments limited to lawmakers who stay aligned, according to Times Brasil citing Folha de S.Paulo. PT president Edinho Silva leads the first round of talks with centrist parties, the MDB could trade about 30 Chamber votes for a ministry, and allies expect the structure by December 20. Names in play include Camilo Santana for Casa Civil or a new Public Security ministry, Gleisi Hoffmann for Social Development, and Piauí governor Rafael Fonteles for Finance.
items.assessment: Paying for votes delivered rather than seats held shifts leverage toward Lula in a Congress he does not control, but it also invites parties to hold back votes until they see the price. The new Congress is sworn in only on February 1, so the cabinet will be built for a legislature that does not yet sit.
items.source: Times Brasil (CNBC licensee), citing Folha de S.Paulo

items.headline: Paraguay: Pedro Alliana sworn in as president after Cartes brokered the succession; Alliana's own impeachment motion was voted down
items.summary: Vice President Pedro Alliana took the oath on November 6 in an extraordinary session of Congress, hours after the Senate removed Santiago Peña over the Ueno Bank collapse; Congress refused Peña's resignation filed the day before. Former president Horacio Cartes, who leads the ruling Colorado Party's dominant Honor Colorado faction, met Alliana after more than a month of distance and negotiated the handover, then backed the case against Peña. A parallel motion to impeach Alliana, over claims he shielded irregularities and backed pension and public fund deposits in Ueno, was rejected. Alliana's first pledge was full compensation for savers, with priority for the poorest.
items.assessment: Power has shifted from a president who had drifted from Cartes back to Cartes's closest loyalist, so the real winner of the Ueno crisis is the ex president under US sanctions since 2023. That raises the question of how Washington handles a government whose kingmaker it has designated for corruption, while Paraguay remains one of Taiwan's few diplomatic allies.

items.headline: Ueno Bank's hole reaches pensioners: about $380 million of Paraguay's social security fund frozen, tied to 32,000 retirees
items.summary: The central bank's resolution of Ueno, a digital bank with about 2.9 million clients and a solvency ratio near 6% against a 12% legal minimum, froze deposits for at least 15 days. About $380 million from the Instituto de Previsión Social, the state pension and health fund, is trapped, linked to roughly 32,000 retirees, and the deposit guarantee covers only about $38,000 per depositor. Eight bank executives have been detained on breach of trust charges.
items.assessment: The guarantee cap protects small savers but not an institutional depositor like the pension fund, so Alliana's promise of full compensation implies a public bailout that will shape Paraguay's budget and credit standing. Who approved parking pension money in a fast growing digital bank is the question that could still reach the new president.

items.headline: Mexico's election authority: 30 resignations after its chair quit, an audit flags 8.87 billion pesos in contracts, and the vote on a successor slips to about November 10
items.summary: The INE (National Electoral Institute) reports 30 resignations since president Guadalupe Taddei quit on October 26, 17 of them from her own office, including the heads of IT, communication and procurement. The federal auditor ASF found 8,870 million pesos in operations from 2014 to 2026 between two business groups and public bodies, 3,790 million of it with electoral authorities, though it assigned no personal blame to Taddei or her predecessor Lorenzo Córdova. Morena's Senate leader Ricardo Monreal delayed approving the call to pick a new INE president to about November 10 after the PAN proposed eight changes.
items.assessment: The purge empties the INE's technical layer seven months before 2027 midterm and judicial elections, and whoever fills it will be chosen by a Congress Morena controls. Monreal seeking PAN consensus he does not need is a bid for legitimacy that can be cited if the new leadership is challenged.

items.headline: Delcy Rodríguez promises an 'economic explosion' decreed by God and unveils 2040 targets
items.summary: At a meeting with community leaders in Maturín, Monagas state, on November 4, acting leader Delcy Rodríguez said an economic boom is coming to Venezuela and that God has already decreed it. The remarks launched a series of official events called Renacer Productivo with economic targets set for 2040. Opposition figures and analysts pointed to failing power and water services and weak wages.
items.assessment: A 2040 horizon from an interim government with no election date tells you how long the managed transition intends to last. It also echoes Maduro's providential language, a sign the Rodríguez team still courts the chavista base even while it works with Washington.

items.headline: teleSUR, still Caracas funded, cheers Peña's fall with street celebrations and a protest slogan
items.summary: Venezuela's state backed network ran Peña's removal and arrest largely in his accusers' words, including a claim that he was the biggest embezzler in Paraguay's history, and closed on crowds chanting 'El pueblo unido jamás será vencido.' It reported a $1.2 billion loss figure from accusers and said Peña was detained at home after prosecutors ordered his arrest. Alliana's side got one line.
items.assessment: Caracas now cooperates with Washington, yet its regional outlet keeps the old line against Paraguay, a US and Taiwan ally. That suggests the media apparatus has not been realigned and remains a lever the Rodríguez government can use abroad while appearing moderate at home.

items.headline: Certificate authority DigiCert says passports and driver's licenses of business customers were exposed
items.summary: DigiCert, a Utah based company that issues the certificates that prove websites are genuine, disclosed that an internal business system moved outside its VPN in February 2025 became reachable from the internet, and an unassigned account was used to access its database in late June 2026; it was fixed by July 2. Exposed data included names, business emails and identity documents such as passports, driver's licenses and utility bills. DigiCert says attackers could not issue certificates and it has no evidence of misuse; the number of affected customers and the attacker are not disclosed.
items.assessment: The documents customers submit to prove identity for high trust certificates are exactly what a forger needs to obtain fraudulent ones elsewhere, so the risk sits downstream at other certificate authorities. The root cause, a migration logged as an infrastructure change and skipped by security review, is a common failure worth flagging to any organization she advises.

items.headline: Canadian extradited for allegedly hijacking university supercomputers in four states to mine crypto

Stubbings is still fighting extradition in Canadian courts. Charges carry up to 10 years.

items.headline: Treasury blacklists eight Canadian money exchangers moving Iranian funds through crypto, some tied to Ryan Wedding drug money
items.summary: On November 6 OFAC designated eight Canada based money services businesses in British Columbia and Ontario under Executive Order 13902, part of an IRGC focused effort called Operation Economic Outcast launched in August. Treasury says they convert rials into digital assets, transacted with already sanctioned Iranian exchanges such as Nobitex and Wallex and with IRGC linked addresses, and changed names and addresses to evade detection; several also laundered proceeds for Canadian trafficker Ryan Wedding. The action was coordinated with FinCEN, Canada's FINTRAC and the DEA, and the list entries include TRX (Tron) wallet addresses.
items.assessment: Publishing Tron addresses lets exchanges and analytics firms freeze funds automatically, so the real effect lands on stablecoin rails, not Canadian bank accounts. Linking Iranian sanctions evasion to a cartel aligned trafficker also gives Washington a narcotics hook to press Ottawa harder, after Bessent said Canada cannot be a safe haven.
items.source: OFAC Recent Actions; Treasury press release sb0686

items.headline: New Cuba sanctions reach two Chinese state defense electronics firms supplying Cuba's military
items.summary: A November 5 State Department action under Cuba Executive Order 14404 designated 8 entities, 2 individuals and 5 vessels. Beyond the family members of GAESA leaders already reported, it hit China National Electronic Import and Export Company (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies, a CETC International subsidiary, for contracting in 2026 with Cuban arms buyer Duna to supply components and surveillance equipment to Cuba's armed forces. It also targeted the Cyprus and Panama owners and managers of Cuban oil tankers (CAROIL, TENTACOOL, PETROMARCA, Internacional Maritima) and blocked the tankers Esperanza, Gloria C, Maria Cristina, Emilia and Lourdes.
items.assessment: Naming major Chinese state defense exporters under a Cuba order widens a Western Hemisphere sanctions tool into US and China competition, and CEIEC was already sanctioned in 2020 for Venezuela surveillance work, showing one supplier serving several allied governments in the region. Blocking named tankers matters more day to day for Cuba's fuel supply than the elite designations.
items.source: State Department fact sheet as reproduced by Defcon Level

items.headline: GEO and CoreCivic post record ICE revenue and say Congress already funded detention through 2029

CoreCivic said revenue rose 27% to over $2 billion with four more centers activated, and its CEO Lucibeth Mayberry noted Congress has funded ICE through 2029. GEO's CEO George Zoley forecast another record quarter.

Watch for Democrats to target the operating contracts rather than the funding.

items.headline: Federalist reads the exit polls the other way: immigration voters still broke Republican

The same polls showed 60% disapproving of how ICE does its job. He warns Republicans against any amnesty deal with the incoming Democratic majorities.
items.assessment: Both camps are right about different numbers: voters trust Republicans on enforcement but dislike ICE's methods, which points to a fight over tactics and oversight rather than deportation levels. That gap is where a Miller led White House and Thompson's committee will collide.

items.headline: Somalia after the ruling: a 30 day clock, a caretaker limit, and the ousted chief justice now says the president threatened him
items.summary: The Supreme Court ruling of November 5 did more than void the term extension. It set the end of parliament's mandate at April 14, 2026 and the president's at May 15, 2026, gave rival camps 30 days to agree an election framework and 90 days to vote, and confined the government to routine caretaker business until then. The court also rejected President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's November 4 dismissal of Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed, saying it bypassed the Judicial Service Commission and parliament; the presidency says the firing answered complaints from judges, staff and lawyers, and maintains the March amendments give it until May 2027 to run one person, one vote elections. A Garowe Online headline dated November 8 reports the ousted chief justice accusing the president of threatening his security.
items.assessment: The 30 day deadline falls around December 5 and is the real tripwire: if no framework emerges, Somalia will have two rival claims to legitimacy (a court that says the state is a caretaker and a presidency that says it is not) at the same moment US and AU attention on al Shabaab is thinning. Watch whether Puntland and Jubaland treat the ruling as license to stop cooperating with Mogadishu on security and revenue.
items.source: The Rio Times (with Garowe Online headline)

items.headline: Nigeria: ADC files appeal and stay against the ruling that voided Atiku's nomination, tells INEC to hold off
items.summary: A day after Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court in Abuja declared the David Mark led caretaker committee of the African Democratic Congress (ADC, the main opposition coalition vehicle) illegal and voided the primary that produced Atiku Abubakar, the party filed a notice of appeal and a motion to stay execution. It formally notified INEC, the electoral commission, and asked it not to take consequential steps while the appeal is pending. The suit was brought by Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former deputy national chairman who argued he should have led the party after chairman Ralph Nwosu resigned. Filing an appeal does not by itself suspend the judgment.
items.assessment: The decisive actor now is INEC, not the courts: if it treats the judgment as live before the stay is heard, Atiku could be off the ballot by administrative default before any appellate ruling, which is why the ADC wrote to INEC first. The ADC and Atiku blame the governing APC for engineering the suit; there is no public evidence either way yet, but intraparty litigation by a disgruntled officer is the standard Nigerian template for knocking out a challenger.

items.headline: Australia sanctions both Burhan and Hemedti, an unusual move by a non traditional actor on Sudan
items.summary: Radio Dabanga reports that Australia on November 6 imposed sanctions and travel bans on four Sudanese individuals, including army chief and transitional leader Abdel Fattah al Burhan and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, citing the war and human rights abuses. The listing treats both sides of the war symmetrically. The other two names were not given in the summary we saw.
items.assessment: Australia has little direct leverage in Sudan, so the significance is signaling: a Five Eyes member listing Burhan at the same time Khartoum is lobbying the UN against Ethiopia undercuts the army's effort to cast itself as the legitimate state facing an external aggressor. It also widens the club of Western states treating both commanders as equally accountable, which narrows Burhan's room to win diplomatic recognition as the sole government.

items.headline: Sudan's drone war shifts to the power grid: UN counts 14 civilians killed and a four day hospital blackout on the White Nile
items.summary: A UN warning reported by Radio Dabanga on November 4 says drone strikes killed at least 14 civilians in El Sunut, Ed Damazin, El Zahour, Khartoum and Abyei, and that strikes on electricity infrastructure are causing widespread harm. In El Dueim, White Nile state, a four day blackout disrupted hospital services. In El Obeid, the besieged capital of North Kordofan, residents report fuel shortages and a lack of drinking water. Earlier in the year a UNDP study put grid damage at about $3 billion.
items.assessment: Targeting transformers and power stations is cheaper and more coercive than taking towns: it shuts hospitals, water pumps and cold chains across a whole state, so the health toll will show up later as cholera and maternal deaths rather than in strike casualty counts. The inclusion of Abyei, the disputed zone between Sudan and South Sudan, shows the drone campaign spilling into an area with a UN mission.

items.headline: Ethiopia: Fano and TPLF leaders appear together on video with the Oromo Liberation Army, as Tigray's interim government runs local polls that bar war veterans
items.summary: The Critical Threats Ethiopia War Security Review (US think tank tracker) reports that on October 31 the 'Alliance for Survival' released a joint video of Fano commander Zemane Kassie and TPLF chairman Debretsion Gebremichael restating the aim of overthrowing the federal government, followed by a written statement with the Oromo Liberation Army. Federal forces reportedly entered Sheraro on November 3 and claim to have captured Tigrayan commanders including Col. Haile Selassie Assefa, described by one analyst as a liaison to Eritrea, while Fano reportedly took Wuchale and Ibnat. Meanwhile the federally backed interim Tigray administration began local elections in Axum and Abiy Addi, with Wazema Radio reporting that veterans of the 2020 to 2022 war and party members are barred from running; civil servant salaries resume November 9. Most battlefield claims are unverified.
items.assessment: Excluding veterans from local office in Tigray effectively excludes most of the TPLF's base, so Addis is building a civilian administration that can claim local legitimacy while the TPLF fights; salaries resuming the same week is the carrot. The three way video matters less militarily than as a recruiting and diaspora fundraising product, and it gives Abiy a single 'insurrection' narrative to justify drone strikes on Amhara, Tigray and Oromia at once.

items.headline: South Africa's metros flip toward the DA: about 40% in Johannesburg, ActionSA second in Tshwane, MK holds eThekwini; final results due November 9
items.summary: Beyond the ANC's collapse to about 32%, early metro counts reported by Eyewitness News show the Democratic Alliance (DA) at about 40% in Johannesburg, 32% in Tshwane, 30% in Ekurhuleni, 45% in Nelson Mandela Bay and 36% in Mangaung, and above 60% in Cape Town, the only metro where it is projected to win outright. ActionSA, Herman Mashaba's party, was at about 23% in Tshwane, and Jacob Zuma's MK party led eThekwini (Durban) at about 34%. EWN separately reported the country could face more than 100 hung councils. The electoral commission is expected to declare final results on Sunday, November 9.
items.assessment: The DA is now the largest party in Gauteng's metros while sitting with the ANC in the national unity government, so every metro coalition deal will test whether it can govern cities against the ANC while partnering with it in Pretoria. MK holding Durban gives Zuma a fiscal and patronage base in the country's main port city ahead of 2029.

items.headline: US now bars anyone who was in Congo in the past 21 days from boarding flights to the United States
items.summary: Since 11:59 p.m. EST on November 3, all international passengers to the US must attest they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the previous 21 days, and anyone who has cannot board a commercial flight to the US, according to CDC guidance summarized by Nature World News. US citizens arriving from Uganda or South Sudan are funneled through designated airports for enhanced screening. CDC says risk to the American public remains low. WHO's standing advice for this outbreak is against travel or trade restrictions.
items.assessment: The rule applies to everyone, not just foreign nationals, so it also catches American aid workers, clinicians and contractors rotating out of the Ebola zone, which raises the personal cost of deploying and may thin the foreign responder pool just as cases accelerate. Attestation based bans historically push travelers to route through third countries and conceal itineraries, which degrades the contact tracing data they are meant to protect.

items.headline: Ebola reaches an eighth Congolese province on the Central African Republic border; about 700 cases and 370 deaths added in nine days
items.summary: US CDC confirmed counts rose from 9,847 cases and 4,761 deaths on October 23 to 10,563 and 5,130 on November 1, with Nord Ubangi now among eight affected provinces; Africa CDC counted 5,376 deaths as of November 2. Kenya's cluster stands at nine cases and two deaths, all in Nairobi and all linked to the first patient, with no community spread reported. Nigeria's single imported case and a close contact were medically evacuated to Switzerland on October 26, per ECDC. Congo has begun testing whether Ervebo, the licensed vaccine for the Zaire strain, gives any cross protection against Bundibugyo; no vaccine or treatment is approved for this strain.
items.assessment: Nord Ubangi and Sud Ubangi sit on the Ubangi river trade route to Bangui, where the health system is far weaker than Uganda's or Kenya's, so the Central African Republic is now the most exposed neighbor and the one least able to detect cases. The Swiss evacuation shows wealthy states will take individual patients, which reassures elites in capitals but does nothing for transmission in Ituri. Agencies' counts already diverge by a few hundred, an early sign of reporting strain.
items.source: Nature World News (citing US CDC, Africa CDC, ECDC)

items.headline: First US bird flu death of 2026: a Yakima County dairy exposure as Washington's cattle outbreak reaches 33 herds
items.summary: A Yakima County, Washington resident with underlying conditions died November 1 after severe avian influenza linked to infected dairy cattle, the first US death this year and the third since 2024. Washington has reported three human cases since mid October, all tied to cows; a third case at a county dairy is mild. The H5N1 cattle outbreak has reached 33 herds in Yakima County plus a dairy in Benton County. Health officer Dave Atteberry says public risk remains low, and contacts of the deceased are being monitored; no sequencing results have been released.
items.assessment: Yakima Valley dairies rely heavily on Latino and often undocumented labor, so with deportations at their current pace, sick workers have strong reasons to avoid testing; three detected cases in a 33 herd outbreak may be an undercount. The absence of published sequences matters most: a fatal case is exactly where mutations for mammalian adaptation would be checked.

items.headline: Democrats line up AI model testing, liability and an AI agency; one analyst says must pass bills are the route
items.summary: Reuters reported Representative Lori Trahan will push bills requiring independent experts to test leading AI models and clarifying company liability for harmful AI actions, Representative Greg Casar wants AI executives to testify under oath, and Senator elect Abdul El-Sayed has called for an independent AI agency. In October, Zoe Lofgren and other House Democratic committee leaders asked OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and SpaceX to detail their security practices and report AI tools acting in unintended ways. Raymond James analyst Ed Mills said legislation is likelier than markets assume, through riders on must pass bills or a veto override push.
items.assessment: The October letters mean Democrats already have a documentary record to build hearings on, so oversight can start in January before any bill passes. Attaching AI rules to spending bills would put Trump in the position of vetoing government funding to protect AI firms.

items.headline: Exit poll: 56% called AI and data centers a major factor; new senators want a moratorium and full energy cost recovery
items.summary: SSRS exit polling cited by The National News Desk found 56% of voters called AI and data centers crucial or major to their vote. Senator elect Annie Andrews of South Carolina backs a two year data center moratorium, Senator elect Roy Cooper of North Carolina wants data centers to pay their full energy cost, and Representative Ted Lieu promised public AI hearings. OpenAI announced commitments on data center energy costs and jobs less than 48 hours after the election and called for clear rules.
items.assessment: OpenAI moving within two days to offer voluntary energy commitments suggests the industry expects to lose on electricity pricing and is trying to set the terms before Congress does. Southern Democrats winning on moratorium platforms makes data centers a bipartisan local issue, not a coastal one.
items.source: The National News Desk (Sinclair) via WJLA

items.headline: Meta, TikTok and Alphabet sue California over a law against 'psychologically exploitative' feeds for kids 15 and under
items.summary: The three companies filed coordinated but separate federal suits in San Jose, San Francisco and Los Angeles against AB 1709, signed by Governor Newsom in September, which bars platforms from deploying addictive design features for users 15 and younger. They argue it violates free speech, conflicts with Section 230, and takes decisions that belong to parents. The law is set to take effect January 1.
items.assessment: Filing three suits in three districts spreads the risk of one bad ruling and raises the odds of conflicting decisions that push the issue to the Ninth Circuit fast. A design based law, not a content law, is the test of whether states can regulate how feeds work rather than what they show.

items.headline: En banc Ninth Circuit rules private groups cannot sue under the Voting Rights Act's voter intimidation clause
items.summary: In SEIU v. Department of Justice, the full Ninth Circuit on November 3 reinstated a panel decision that Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act, which bars intimidating voters, gives private parties no right to sue, and denied rehearing the same day. On November 4 the district court in San Francisco stayed the union's preliminary injunction bid while the government's appeal is pending. The case concerned DOJ election day activity in California.
items.assessment: If this holds, only the Justice Department can enforce the intimidation clause, which means the agency accused of intimidation is the sole plaintiff allowed to bring the claim. A new Democratic Congress could fix it by statute, which makes a private right of action an early test of whether Democrats legislate or only investigate.
items.source: Just Security, 2026 Midterms Election Integrity Litigation Tracker

items.headline: Boasberg rejects DHS bid to punish plaintiffs over the voter list they obtained in discovery
items.summary: In Trujillo and Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights v. DHS, Chief Judge James Boasberg in Washington on November 3 denied the government's motion claiming plaintiffs violated a court order in handling a list of voters disclosed in discovery. The suit challenges DHS's effort to match voter rolls against immigration data to find suspected noncitizen voters.
items.assessment: The government trying to sanction plaintiffs over the list suggests it sees the matched data itself as sensitive, which is the core question the case will decide: what DHS may do with state voter files. That record will matter when Democratic committees ask for the same data.
items.source: Just Security, 2026 Midterms Election Integrity Litigation Tracker

items.headline: War on the Rocks: killing Iran's top leaders made Tehran harder to deal with, not easier
items.summary: War on the Rocks' members newsletter says that with the US midterms over, the US and Iranian standoff is stuck and the next move belongs to Washington. It lists a munitions shortage and a public that does not want renewed war as practical limits on a new campaign. A companion podcast with former CIA analyst Cole Bucy argues Iran's leadership changed in kind when Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed on the war's first day in February, so Tehran now gains little by playing it safe.
items.assessment: The decapitation strike is usually scored as a US success; this reading treats it as the reason talks stall, because the survivors have watched years of forecast economic collapse fail to arrive and believe they can absorb more pain. It also flags that Trump may see little downside in going back to war now that the vote is behind him.
items.source: War on the Rocks (The Adversarial newsletter; The Insider podcast)

items.headline: Kyiv's forecasts of 30,000 to 100,000 more North Korean troops never materialized
items.summary: Writing in the Lowy Institute's Interpreter, Boston College researcher Khang Vu tracks Ukrainian warnings that rose from up to 100,000 extra North Korean soldiers (November 2024) to 50,000 (August 2026); none arrived. He puts the current force at 14,000 to 16,000, about 9,500 of them active duty soldiers in artillery, rocket and drone roles around Kursk. A North Korean laborer reportedly earns about $7,500 a year versus about $24,000 for a soldier, and the arms trade with Russia is valued at $14.4 billion.
items.assessment: Pyongyang has already banked combat experience and a weapons showroom, so laborers and shells now earn it more hard currency at lower political risk than more bodies at the front. For analysts, it is a case study in how a belligerent's threat inflation can become accepted fact through repetition.

items.headline: Pakistan briefly barred Taiwan's two big airlines from its airspace under the One China policy
items.summary: In October Pakistan reportedly denied overflight to China Airlines and EVA Air, Taiwan's two main carriers; Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said only mainland China is allowed under the One China policy. The ban was quickly reversed and access restored until March 27, 2027, with no word on what happens after. Beijing itself does not restrict Taiwanese airlines this way.
items.assessment: Islamabad went further than Beijing asks, likely to signal loyalty to China while it courts Washington, and the open ended March 2027 date leaves a lever in place. Because Taiwan is excluded from the UN civil aviation body, any copycat move by other China aligned states would force costly reroutes on flights to Europe and the Middle East.

items.headline: A former Biden aide argues the midterm loss leaves Trump's foreign policy hand largely intact
items.summary: Cory Alpert, a University of Melbourne researcher who spent three years in the Biden White House, argues Democrats' gains repudiated tariffs and the Iran war as cost of living issues, yet Trump keeps unilateral foreign policy control until January 2029. Democrats gain the budget process and investigative power, including probes of corporate executives with foreign government deals. Foreign governments, he says, now have reason to hedge for two full years.
items.assessment: The usual lame duck story assumes Congress reins in war and trade; Alpert's point is that the real effect may be foreign capitals stalling on deals with a divided Washington, which slows diplomacy even where the White House still acts alone.

items.headline: War on the Rocks names a new class of defense contractor: the 'neo primes'
items.summary: A November 2 essay by journalist Sharon Weinberger and analyst Jonathan Panter examines how technology companies are becoming major Pentagon contractors alongside the traditional prime contractors. Only the title and byline were checked; the full argument was not read.
items.assessment: Worth tracking because a Democratic Congress now controls appropriations and has signaled scrutiny of AI firms; the defense budget is where tech capex and political risk meet.

items.headline: Markets now price a December Fed rate hike at about 77% as the Bank of England raises to 4%
items.summary: After October payrolls beat forecasts by more than double and unemployment fell to 4.1%, futures put the odds of a Federal Reserve hike in December near 77%, up from 67% a day earlier, with one more hike priced for 2027. The Bank of England raised its rate to 4.0% after six cuts last year. Wage growth slowed to 3.1%, below forecast.
items.assessment: The war's oil shock is turning into a tightening cycle in the middle of a tech selloff, the opposite of the usual flight to easier money. Ten year inflation breakevens at 2.24%, the softest since early August, suggest bond traders doubt the hikes are needed, a split worth watching.

items.headline: Bank of England reportedly questions lenders on loans to data centers with no tenant signed
items.summary: Citing Bloomberg, BullionVault reports the UK central bank is asking banks about lending to data center projects that have no tenant in place. The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.5% on November 5, its steepest single day drop in more than 18 months, and sat 9% below its October 6 record; about $6 trillion was erased from equity markets in the week.
items.assessment: Speculative data centers built before a cloud or AI customer signs are the credit side of the AI boom that equity coverage misses; a regulator asking questions is how a valuation story becomes a bank exposure story.

items.headline: Bitcoin traded like a tech stock, not like gold, in the week's rout
items.summary: Bitcoin fell more than 6% on November 5 to $75,463 on Bitstamp, its lowest since September 16, briefly breaking its 50 week average. Crypto liquidations neared $850 million in 24 hours, per CoinGlass. Gold, by contrast, rose 4.1% for the week to about $4,050 an ounce.
items.assessment: The 'digital gold' pitch failed its live test again: under stress Bitcoin moved with the Nasdaq while bullion caught the safety bid, which matters for anyone treating it as a hedge against the war or the Fed.

items.headline: Vietnam's other trade pacts could hand Washington's concessions to its rivals
items.summary: Law lecturer Tran Hoang Tu Linh notes Vietnam signed a trade deal with EFTA (Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) on October 18 whose Article 4.4 requires equal treatment for EFTA service suppliers. The CPTPP Pacific trade pact has similar clauses. If the pending US deal lets American investors exceed Vietnam's 49% cap on foreign ownership in facilities based telecoms, Japanese, Australian or Canadian investors could demand the same.
items.assessment: Most favored nation clauses mean US bilateral wins may not stay American, so Washington could pay for openings that its competitors also get; no text of the US deal has been published to check.

items.headline: Oil fell about 13% on the week as traders priced a Democratic Congress as pressure for an Iran deal
items.summary: Brazil's Jornal do Comércio reports Brent for January settled at $98.32 and WTI for December at $90.83 on November 6, with futures down about 13% over the week. The paper attributes the slide to bets that the Democratic win gives Washington more reason to seek a diplomatic exit, while noting a peace deal remains distant amid continued Gulf attacks.
items.assessment: The market is treating a domestic US election as a war risk event, which means the price now carries a political premium that can reverse on a single strike headline, as it did on November 5 when tanker attacks lifted Brent 2.5% in a day.

items.headline: US gasoline hits its 2026 low at $4.10, but only a fraction of crude's drop reached the pump
items.summary: The AAA national average was $4.10 a gallon on November 5, down from $4.17 on November 2, yet still about 34% above the $3.06 Thanksgiving 2025 average. Only about 7 cents of a potential 18 to 24 cent decline had passed through. Analyst Tom Kloza warned refined product prices may stay high well after crude eases.
items.assessment: Refinery and product tightness, not crude, is now the binding constraint, so a ceasefire would lower pump prices slower than voters expect, which matters for the affordability politics that decided the midterms.

items.headline: Argentina takes the UK to the law of the sea tribunal over the Falklands' Sea Lion oil field; hearings November 10 and 11
items.summary: Argentina has asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg for provisional measures against the UK's approval of the Sea Lion offshore project, about 107 nautical miles north of the Falklands (Malvinas), licensed to Navitas Petroleum with Rockhopper Exploration. A full arbitral case would follow. International law professor Donald Rothwell says the tribunal cannot rule on sovereignty, which the claim depends on.
items.assessment: This is Buenos Aires turning a sovereignty dispute into an environmental and maritime rights case, the same route Mauritius used on Chagos; even a loss could chill financing for the first Falklands oil development.

items.headline: Silver up 6.3% from its 2026 low as copper slides; metals split on war and rate bets
items.summary: Silver traded near $51.80 an ounce on November 6, up 6.3% from Monday's low for the year, while copper fell 3.5% on the week. Gold rose 4.1% from a 13 month closing low the previous Friday.
items.assessment: Industrial copper falling while precious metals rise is a classic growth scare signal, at odds with the strong jobs report that pushed rate hike bets higher.

items.headline: COP31 opens November 9 in Antalya under an unusual split presidency
items.summary: The UN climate summit runs November 9 to 20 in Antalya: Türkiye hosts and runs the voluntary Action Agenda, Australia manages the formal negotiations, and Türkiye insists it has the final say. Türkiye will launch a pledge on November 10 for electricity to supply 35% of final energy by 2035, up from about 23 to 24% today. Climate Action Tracker projects only about 28% under current policies.
items.assessment: The electrification pledge does not require that the power be clean, so a country could meet it with gas plants; critics read it as a way to avoid a fossil fuel signal. Deforestation has also been almost entirely cut from the host's agenda, a quiet reversal from last year's Amazon summit.

items.headline: Brazil publishes a 182 page voluntary fossil fuel roadmap with a 2033 timetable
items.summary: Released November 3, Brazil's roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels sets a timetable to 2033. European and small island states may try to reference it in the COP31 cover decision, while producer states oppose it. Brazilian officials say it is not a formal document requiring negotiation.
items.assessment: Brasília keeps the credit for ambition while declining to make it binding; the fight over a single citation will show where the fossil phase out debate really stands.

items.headline: The IPCC still cannot agree when its next major reports are due, after a sixth failed attempt
items.summary: Governments are split on whether the IPCC's seventh assessment reports (AR7) will be ready for the 2028 global stocktake, the five yearly review of the Paris Agreement. The panel's last meeting was suspended after a sixth failure to agree on a timeline. The question will come up at Antalya.
items.assessment: Delay is a policy choice: if the science arrives after the 2028 stocktake, governments review their progress without the newest evidence, which suits states resisting tougher targets.

items.headline: Loss and damage fund holds $342 million against $2.8 billion in first requests
items.summary: A German Green Party foundation briefing says the UN fund for climate loss and damage has a $342 million startup phase while initial requests total $2.8 billion. It also says adaptation finance was $31.7 billion in 2024, mostly loans, against an annual gap of about $387 billion. Lowering global temperature by 0.1°C after overshoot would need about 200 billion tonnes of CO2 removed, four to five years of global emissions.
items.assessment: Adaptation money arriving as loans, some at market rates, adds debt to the most exposed countries, so climate finance can deepen the very fiscal crises that limit adaptation.

items.headline: Amendment 3 passed with about 62%; Lee County's own staff projected $121 million then $159 million in cuts
items.summary: Florida voters approved Amendment 3 with roughly 62%, above the 60% threshold; it raises the homestead exemption on non school property taxes by $150,000 next year and $250,000 in 2028. In a September workshop Lee County staff projected required cuts of $121 million in 2027 and 2028 and $159 million the following year, with public safety, animal services, parks and the 20/20 land buying program at risk. Options laid out included new taxing units (MSTUs), higher user fees, bonds or a higher millage rate; Commissioner Cecil Pendergrass noted residents may still pay through fees. Separately, state general revenue came in $429 million above projections in September.
items.assessment: The relief goes to homesteaded owners while renters, newer buyers and businesses keep paying, and the likely local response, fees and special taxing units, shifts costs to people who did not get the exemption. The state's revenue surplus is the pot the Legislature can use to soften the blow, which gives Tallahassee new leverage over counties.

items.headline: DeSantis promises a property tax special session with a grant pool for rural sheriffs, and another Citizens rate cut
items.summary: DeSantis said the Legislature will set dates for a special session to implement Amendment 3 by January 1, including a schedule of further homestead relief, limits on local governments raising revenue other ways to get around it, and a grant pool worth tens of millions for core needs such as rural sheriffs. School districts are excluded. He also announced another auto insurance rebate and said he expects Citizens Property Insurance to cut rates again in South Florida by year end or early next year.
items.assessment: Capping local workarounds while handing out state grants converts county independence into dependence on Tallahassee, a meaningful shift for Lee County after a year of fights with the state over budgets. The Citizens forecast is the governor's claim and should be checked against the insurer's own filings.

items.headline: Cape Coral elects retired Green Beret Rick Erickson mayor by 2,840 votes
items.summary: Rick Erickson, 63, a 32 year Army veteran, won about 52% against Lisa Cohen-Adkinson, who said he won with distortions and personal attacks. He is set to be sworn in as the city's 17th mayor on November 18. Incumbent John Gunter, appointed in 2021 after Mayor Joe Coviello's death, finished third of seven in the primary.
items.assessment: With Fort Myers also replacing its mayor, both of Lee County's biggest cities change leadership right as Amendment 3 cuts hit city budgets, so the first test for new mayors will be fees and service cuts, not campaign themes.

items.headline: Patrick Lawrence: AIPAC's exit from direct endorsements is a retreat into shell PACs, not a surrender
items.summary: In a Consortium News column, Patrick Lawrence argues that AIPAC's October decision to stop endorsing candidates and giving directly moves its money into short lived and shell political action committees (PACs, groups that raise and spend campaign money) that hide donors. He points to the Michigan Senate primary, where Abdul El-Sayed beat Mike Rogers 52 to 48 after AIPAC aligned money backed Haley Stevens, and to a pending defense bill provision he calls NDAA Section 219.
items.assessment: If the shell PAC model holds, the next fight is over disclosure law rather than lobby endorsements, which puts the FEC and state campaign finance regulators, not Congress, at the center of the Israel lobbying debate in 2028.
items.support: NPR's report quoting AIPAC's letter to members; an Al Jazeera investigation by Ali Harb into Chicago shell PACs that Lawrence says moved about $7.3 million to split progressive votes; a Drop Site News report that two Rogers staffers are registered foreign agents for Israel.
items.against: AIPAC's own stated reason is that it is ending endorsements and direct giving; no rebuttal from AIPAC to the shell PAC claim was found in the window. Lawrence's reading of AIPAC's motives is his interpretation.

items.headline: Jeffrey Sachs: the midterms were a referendum on the Iran war, so peace is now good politics
items.summary: Economist Jeffrey Sachs argues voters punished the Iran war and its costs and that Democrats should run on an antiwar platform: reclaim war and spending powers, settle Ukraine on neutrality terms, end support for Israel's wars and cut the military budget. He cites the AP voter survey showing about 60% called the use of force against Iran wrong and about 90% named cost of living a major factor, plus gasoline rising from about $2.80 to a $4.43 monthly average by September.
items.assessment: The same 'the war lost the election' frame is now being argued from the antiwar left (Sachs), the populist right (ZeroHedge) and the White House (Vance), which makes it the most bipartisan explanation of the result and a pressure point on Democratic leaders who backed tougher Iran policy.
items.support: AP voter survey figures on the Iran war and cost of living; gasoline and 10 year Treasury yield data; a May 2026 NYT and Siena poll on Democratic voters and Israel aid.
items.against: Sachs' own figure that about 90% named cost of living suggests prices, not the war itself, may be the driver. Conservative commentator Erick Erickson blamed immigration enforcement leaders (Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, Corey Lewandowski) for losing Hispanic voters, a competing explanation (via Media Matters, Nov 6).

items.headline: Providence voters pass a 75% divestment ordinance, making it the largest US city to divest from Israel
items.summary: Providence, Rhode Island voters approved Question 7, a citizen initiated ordinance, with about 75% on November 3. It orders the city to divest from companies and countries profiting from genocide, apartheid or prolonged occupation, without naming Israel; local activists say the city holds millions in Israel Bonds. The coalition gathered over 10,000 signatures after outgoing Mayor Brett Smiley blocked a council version.
items.assessment: A ballot route around a mayor's block is a replicable template; watch for copycat initiatives and for Rhode Island legislators testing whether state anti boycott rules can override a voter passed ordinance.
items.support: Certified election tally of the Question 7 vote; signature drive by the Providence for Palestine Coalition; Jewish Voice for Peace Rhode Island figures on Israel Bonds holdings.
items.against: None found in the article; no state legal challenge or statement from Jewish community groups was reported in the window.

items.headline: Moon of Alabama predicts a lame duck Trump may strike Iran around the November 8 to 9 new moon
items.summary: The blogger known as 'b' at Moon of Alabama, a German run anti establishment site focused on war coverage, wrote that Trump might renew strikes on Iran around the new moon because the military prefers darkness. He says outright he does not know, and argues a weakened Trump may want a dramatic legacy act while the Democratic congressional leadership will not change policy much.
items.assessment: This is the left side twin of right wing Doomsday Plane chatter: both read routine military signals as countdowns, and both will be retroactively scored against what happens this week, which is how such blogs build or lose credibility with their audience.
items.support: The general military preference for night operations and the lunar calendar; Trump's political position after the midterms. Troop movement and tanker flight claims appear only in reader comments, not the post.
items.against: On November 8 Trump told CNN's Jim Sciutto that new strikes are 'highly unlikely' if Iran signs a strong agreement, while keeping the option open; indirect talks through Qatari and Gulf mediators continue.

items.headline: Moon of Alabama: Stephen Miller's promotion protects Defense Secretary Hegseth
items.summary: Moon of Alabama argues that naming Stephen Miller White House chief of staff shields Pete Hegseth from being made the scapegoat for the Iran war and the midterm loss. The post leans on a New York Times account of Miller's role, Hegseth's public congratulations and reporting on the two men's close social ties.
items.assessment: If correct, the Pentagon leadership that ran the Iran campaign survives intact into the Democratic Congress, which raises the odds of a direct oversight clash with the incoming Armed Services Democrats rather than a quiet personnel reset.
items.support: A New York Times report on Miller's new role; Hegseth's posts congratulating Miller; reporting on their personal ties.
items.against: None found; the White House has given its own reasons for the appointment, framed around continuity of the policy agenda.

items.headline: Georgia's secretary of state finds an uncounted memory card that flips a state House seat to the Republican
items.summary: A routine check after the election found about 388 more voters checked in than ballots reported in Seminole County, part of southwest Georgia's House District 154. Counting the missed Election Day memory card turned Democrat Harry James' 58 vote lead into a 262 vote lead for Republican Gerald Greene. Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger called the failure unacceptable and opened an investigation; ZeroHedge relayed the AJC, WCTV and The Current.
items.assessment: This is a documented counting error discovered by the system's own audit, and it helped the Republican: expect both camps to cite it, one as proof that audits work and the other as proof that more errors are hiding in places that were not audited.
items.support: Secretary of State announcement and audit finding; state results showing Greene 10,193 to James 9,932; local reporting by the AJC, WCTV and The Current.
items.against: Officials say the error was caught by the normal post election reconciliation process; no claim of intentional manipulation has been made by officials.

items.headline: City Journal sting: an LA immigrant rights group hosted an official voting center while staff recommended candidates
items.summary: Christopher Rufo and two colleagues report that CHIRLA, a Los Angeles immigrant rights nonprofit that has received over $100 million in California funds since 2019, hosted an official county voting center during a get out the vote event where an employee walked them through which candidates to pick. They argue this may break California's 100 foot electioneering rule and federal limits on 501(c)(3) charities, and urge the IRS and Treasury to act. ZeroHedge republished the piece.
items.assessment: This gives the right a concrete, nameable target after a loss it cannot plausibly blame on mass fraud, and a regulatory lever (IRS status) the administration controls directly; watch for a Treasury or IRS move against CHIRLA as the first test of post election retaliation against Democratic aligned groups.
items.support: The authors' undercover visit; LA County registrar records confirming CHIRLA hosted a county voting center; California Elections Code and IRS guidance on charity political activity.
items.against: CHIRLA says its civic engagement staff are trained to give clear, accurate guidance and calls the story another attack by anti immigrant opponents; it also runs a separate 501(c)(4) arm that may legally endorse. No recording was published.

items.headline: Kunstler on ZeroHedge: the midterms were a fraud built to launch a 'color revolution'
items.summary: Novelist and blogger James Howard Kunstler claims Democrats registered ineligible and fictitious voters to flood the count with mail ballots, then plan riots and a push to declare Trump illegitimate, possibly leading to the Insurrection Act. He says a DOJ voter roll audit will expose it, and alleges Minnesota fraud involving Peggy Flanagan and Tim Walz.
items.assessment: The 'color revolution' frame recasts a lost election as a foreign style regime change operation, which is the rhetorical groundwork for emergency measures; its spread matters more than its content if the DOJ roll audit produces any headline number.
items.support: Kunstler cites unnamed people on recorded Zoom calls and the pending DOJ voter roll audit; no statistics are given.
items.against: Michigan's Department of State and AP Fact Focus found no record of the Election Day irregularities circulating online; Media Matters (Nov 5) documented that emergency orders, ICE at polls and similar plans did not happen; Georgia's one confirmed counting error favored a Republican.

items.headline: Epoch Times: Trump backs Nvidia's Jensen Huang despite a probe into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy
items.summary: The Epoch Times, a paper founded by Falun Gong followers and hostile to Beijing, reports that Nvidia's board opened a probe into whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence after he admitted an affair with 'Alice Huang', an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore firm that is a major Nvidia customer. Trump called Huang honorable, said he had heard of no wrongdoing and floated bringing him on next week's China trip. Rubio called it an internal corporate matter.
items.assessment: Trump's defense of Huang puts him at odds with the China hawk wing that dominates outlets like Epoch Times; the story gives export control hardliners in a Democratic Congress a bipartisan opening to tighten chip sales just as Trump heads to Beijing.
items.support: Nvidia's announced board probe; Huang's admission of the affair; the reported Megaspeed customer link.
items.against: Trump says he has heard nothing showing wrongdoing; Rubio declined comment; the article does not name the original outlet behind the espionage allegation.

items.headline: War Room: Bannon says 'caravans' are already moving after the Democratic win
items.summary: On War Room, Steve Bannon's daily show on Real America's Voice, Bannon said on November 4 that caravans were already heading north and that Central Americans believed the gates were open again, without sourcing. Laura Ingraham, Brian Kilmeade, The Gateway Pundit and Alex Jones' site carried versions the same week, according to Media Matters.
items.assessment: The pivot from fraud to invasion lets the movement explain a loss without disputing the count, and it hands the lame duck Congress a reason to rush border legislation before January.
items.source: Media Matters (on War Room, Fox News, Gateway Pundit)
items.support: Bannon cited no source; The Gateway Pundit cited Fox reporter Bill Melugin's analysis; caravan warnings had aired in September and October before the vote.
items.against: Media Matters found no reporting confirming a new caravan; no Honduran, Guatemalan or Mexican government statement on a caravan was found in the window.

items.headline: Former CIA officer Kiriakou: the agency told the White House three times that Iran had no bomb program
items.summary: On Judge Andrew Napolitano's libertarian show Judging Freedom, former CIA officer John Kiriakou said three separate national intelligence estimates before the war concluded Iran had no nuclear weapons program, and that analysts judged the war a mistake. He also cited a leaked CIA 'red cell' paper suggesting Israel, not Iran, could break apart. ZeroHedge carried the segment, which also featured former analyst Larry Johnson.
items.assessment: Kiriakou and Johnson both signed the VIPS 'Iran Is Not Bluffing' memo; this is the same small network pushing its case through a right libertarian channel, which is how the antiwar left message is now reaching MAGA skeptics of the war.
items.support: Kiriakou says it rests partly on leaks; DNI Tulsi Gabbard's March 2025 testimony that Iran was not building a weapon; no estimate document was published.
items.against: The administration's case for the war rests on Iran's enrichment level and stockpile; no official confirmation that three estimates exist was found.
